# Silex — Stop Gambling

An iPhone app that blocks gambling across the phone, runs a 90-day evidence-based quit program, and tracks the money you keep. No accounts, no ads, and nothing a user writes leaves the phone. Built by Kyrylo Lozovyi. Weekly $4.99 or annual $49.99 with a 3-day free trial.

Silex is a wellness app, not medical care, and does not diagnose or treat any condition.

Index: https://trysilex.com/llms.txt

# Quit gambling for good. Keep the money.
URL: https://trysilex.com/
Language: en
Description: Silex blocks gambling across your iPhone, walks you through a 90-day evidence-based quit program, and counts the money you keep. No accounts, no ads, no profile of you.

Silex is an iPhone app that blocks gambling across your whole phone, walks you through 90 days one at a time, and counts the money you didn't lose. No accounts. No ads. No profile of you. Ever.
- Private by design
- Evidence-based
- No ads. Ever.
- iPhone, iOS 17+

## Four things, done properly

### Five layers of blocking
A system-wide DNS shield that covers every app and browser, a Safari content blocker built on a bundled list of hundreds of thousands of gambling domains, plus guided setup for the three defences that actually hold: operator self-exclusion, a bank gambling block, and killing every promo email and push.
How this compares to other blockers · The full iPhone blocking guide

### A real 90-day program
90 authored days in three phases — See the Machine, Rewire, Fortify — built from clinical CBT workbooks and the research on how gambling products are designed to hook you. One lesson a day, not a library to binge.
Every source we built it from

### An SOS for the worst minute
One button, always on screen, never behind the paywall. Rate the urge, breathe it down, then ride it out on a timer while the app shows you your own reasons for quitting and the money you've kept so far.
Why urges pass, and how long it takes

### The money, made visible
Not gambled away. Silex takes what you told it you were putting in each week and counts up what you kept instead. It's the number that keeps people going when motivation runs out.
Work out what gambling has cost you so far

## It never punishes you for slipping
Gambling recovery is not a clean line, and an app that zeroes your progress the moment you lapse teaches you to hide the lapse. Silex does the opposite. A slip triggers a Reset day — a specific lesson about what happened and what to change — and your history is never wiped. Milestones you've earned are never taken back.
What to do in the hour after you gamble again

## What it costs, plainly
Silex is a paid app and it tells you so before you invest any time: after the intake questions you reach a paywall. $4.99 per week, or $49.99 per year with a 3-day free trial — about $0.96 a week. Cancel any time in your Apple account settings.
Three things stay free forever, with or without a subscription: the urge button, the crisis helplines, and lapse support. Those are safety features, and safety features should never sit behind a payment screen.

## Private because there is nothing to identify you by
No account, no email, no password, no ad network, nothing that follows you between apps. Your answers, your spending figures, your journal and your lapses live on your phone, with an optional iCloud backup encrypted to your Apple account — we cannot read any of it. The one thing Silex sends is an anonymous count of which setup steps get finished, so what trips people up can be fixed. One switch in Settings turns it off.
The full privacy policy

## Common questions

Q: Is Silex free?
A: The safety tools are free forever — the urge button, the crisis helplines and the lapse support work without paying. The 90-day program and the protection stack need a subscription: $4.99 a week, or $49.99 a year with a 3-day free trial.

Q: Does Silex work on Android?
A: Not yet. Silex is iPhone-only, iOS 17 or later. It uses iOS-specific system APIs — DNS profiles, Safari content blockers, Screen Time — that have no direct Android equivalent.

Q: Can I remove the blocking in a moment of craving?
A: You can, and Silex is honest about that: no app can make itself truly unremovable on iOS. That is exactly why it layers five defences instead of relying on one, and why the strongest layer it points you at is operator self-exclusion, which you cannot undo on impulse.

Q: Does Silex send my data anywhere?
A: Almost nothing. There are no accounts, and everything you write stays on your phone with an optional private iCloud backup that only you can read. The app does send an anonymous count of which setup steps get finished, so the places people get stuck can be fixed — one switch in Settings turns that off.

Q: Is Silex medical treatment?
A: No. Silex helps you build healthier habits around gambling. It is not medical care and doesn't diagnose or treat any condition. If you are in crisis, use the helplines below.

# Who builds Silex
URL: https://trysilex.com/about/
Language: en
Description: Silex is built by one developer, Kyrylo Lozovyi, in Kyiv. No investors, no growth team, nothing that profiles you — and a short list of rules the app will not break.

I built this because I watched someone close to me go through it, and at the time there wasn't much I could actually do. So this is me being useful a bit late.
Quick honesty: I'm not a doctor, and there's no company here. It's one person — Kyrylo Lozovyi, an iOS developer in Kyiv. No investors, no growth team, no data science department — the only thing the app reports back is which setup steps get finished, and even that is anonymous and switchable off.
When it's someone you know, you start reading. I went down a rabbit hole on how betting apps are actually designed — the near-misses, the losses dressed up as wins with a little celebration sound, the whole thing tuned to keep you on the screen. Once you've seen it you can't unsee it. It's not a fair fight. One person is up against a building full of people paid to keep them betting, and we act like willpower should be enough to win that.
So I spent a few weeks of nights building the other side of it. No investors, no ads, no server sitting somewhere with your worst nights on it. And one rule from day one: nothing in this app spins, nothing is random, nothing ever gives you a near-miss. That stuff works — that's exactly why it's not going anywhere near a recovery app.
If it helps you keep your money, it did its job.
Silex isn't the only thing I build this way. VitalityRise is a men's pelvic floor training app on the same rules — no accounts, no claim to treat anything, every number traced to a paper. Different subject, same refusal to bluff.

## How it got built
Silex started in July 2026 as a native iOS app and shipped as version 1.0 in August 2026. The 90-day program was written first, from clinical and academic sources, and the app was built around it — not the other way round. Every screen is SwiftUI; the milestone pieces are rendered with Metal shaders; there is no backend holding your data.
Being a solo developer has one real disadvantage worth naming: there is no support team, so replies to support@trysilex.com come from me, sometimes a day later. It also has an advantage that matters more in this category: nobody has to grow a number this quarter, so nothing in the app is designed to keep you opening it longer than you need it.

## Rules the app doesn't break
These were fixed before the first line of code and have survived every redesign since:
- Nothing playable, ever. No slot animation you can spin, no randomised reward, no near-miss, no mystery box, no fear of missing out. Gambling products work by dosing uncertainty, and a recovery app that borrows those mechanics is feeding the thing it claims to treat. The cold open in onboarding shows a machine playing itself precisely so you cannot touch it.
- The panic button is never paywalled. Neither are the crisis helplines or the lapse support. Charging someone for the worst sixty seconds of their month is indefensible.
- No shame mechanics. Your history is never zeroed. A lapse triggers a lesson, not a punishment, and every milestone you earn is permanent.
- Wellness language, never diagnosis. The app is explicit that it isn't medical care and that its self-check is a snapshot of risk, not a diagnosis.
- Helplines get re-verified every release. They are the one part of the app where a stale number could do real harm.

## What Silex is not
It is not treatment, not therapy, and not a substitute for either. If gambling has put you in debt you cannot service, or you are having thoughts of harming yourself, the right next step is a person, not an app — the numbers below are free and answer 24/7.

## Contact
Support and press: support@trysilex.com. Privacy questions are answered in the privacy policy, which is unusually detailed on purpose.

# The best gambling blocker apps, compared honestly
URL: https://trysilex.com/best-gambling-blocker-apps/
Language: en
Description: Gamban, BetBlocker, GamBlock and the rest — what each one covers, what it costs, and which to pick. Prices verified from each vendor's own site, with a disclosure: we make one of these.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: BetBlocker is free, run by a registered charity, and the right first install for almost everyone. Gamban (£4.99/month or £29.99/year) is the strongest cross-platform blocker if you gamble on more than a phone. Silex — which we make, so weigh that — is for people who want the 90-day quit program alongside the blocking. Whichever you choose, a blocker on its own is the weakest of the three layers that matter; the other two are self-exclusion and a bank block, and both are free.

Disclosure first, because it changes how you should read this: we make Silex, one of the apps below. So this page does two things to stay useful — it names what each competitor does better, and it verifies every price against the vendor's own website rather than repeating other roundups. Prices below were checked on 10 August 2026.

## How these were assessed
- Coverage: does it block every app and browser, or only Safari?
- Platforms: phone only, or computer too?
- Removal resistance: how long does undoing it take at 1am?
- List maintenance: who keeps the domain list current — you or them?
- Honesty of claims: does the marketing promise things iOS cannot do?
- What happens after the block: does anything help you actually stop, or does the product end at the wall?

## The comparison
App | Price | Platforms | Best for
BetBlocker | Free, forever, no ads | iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, Linux, Fire OS | The first thing anyone should install
Gamban | £4.99/month or £29.99/year, 7-day free trial | iOS, Android, Windows, Mac | Gambling across phone and computer
GamBlock | Paid; not published on the homepage | Windows, Mac/iOS, Android | Maximum removal resistance on Windows/Android
Silex (ours) | $4.99/week or $49.99/year, 3-day trial | iPhone only | Blocking plus a structured 90-day program
iOS Screen Time | Free, built in | iPhone, iPad | Stopping reinstalls; needs someone else to hold the passcode

## BetBlocker — free, and not a lesser option
BetBlocker is a charity project: founded by the dispute-resolution service ThePOGG in 2017 and established as an independent charity registered in Scotland (SC049565) in 2019. It costs "absolutely nothing. Ever.", carries no ads, and states it blocks 356,000+ gambling websites and 1,900+ apps for more than 105,000 active users.
Its best feature is the one paid apps often lack: you can set a restriction period from one day up to five years and you cannot shorten it once it starts. That's a real commitment device, given away.
Where it's weaker: it is a blocker and nothing else — no program, no urge tools, no money tracking. Setup is more manual than a polished commercial app. But if you install exactly one thing today, install this, and only pay for something else if you find a gap it leaves.
Source: betblocker.org, checked 10 August 2026.

## Gamban — the cross-platform choice
Gamban charges £4.99 billed monthly or £29.99 billed annually, with a 7-day free trial and no payment up front. One subscription covers iOS, Android, Windows and Mac. It advertises blocking, progress monitoring, layered self-exclusion and on-demand technical support.
Why it's worth the money for some people: gambling rarely stays on one device. If your pattern includes a laptop at night, Gamban covers both under one licence, and it detects new gambling sites rather than relying purely on a static list.
Where it's weaker: like every blocker, it can't defeat iOS's own rules — removal on an iPhone is a Settings trip. And there's no recovery content: it walls the door, then hands the rest back to you.
A note on other roundups: several currently list Gamban at £24.99/year. That figure is out of date; the pricing page says £29.99. It's a small thing that tells you how much of this niche's content is copied rather than checked.
Source: gamban.com/pricing, checked 10 August 2026. Full Gamban alternatives comparison →

## GamBlock — the heaviest lock, on the right platforms
GamBlock takes a different technical approach, using heuristics to identify gambling sites rather than "the simple lists imitators use that are never up to date", in its own words. On Windows and Android it claims removal "cannot happen" and that it blocks factory resets; for Apple devices it claims the protection survives a factory reset.
Consider it if your risk is a Windows PC and you want the least removable option available.
Two caveats. Its pricing isn't shown on the homepage, which makes comparison shopping annoying, and strong removal-resistance claims deserve testing on your own hardware during any refund window. We have not independently verified them.
Source: gamblock.com, checked 10 August 2026. Claims are the vendor's, not ours.

## Silex — ours, so read this sceptically
Silex is iPhone-only, $4.99/week or $49.99/year with a 3-day trial. It installs an encrypted-DNS shield that covers every app and browser, ships a Safari content blocker built on a large bundled domain list, and walks you through setting up the layers it can't provide itself — self-exclusion, a bank block, killing promo emails.
The actual reason it exists is the other half: a 90-day program written from clinical CBT material, an always-available urge button that is never paywalled, and a counter for the money you kept. Blocking buys ninety seconds; the program is about what you do with them.
Where it loses to the apps above: iPhone only — no Android, no desktop. It costs more than BetBlocker, which is free. And it is new, with none of Gamban's operating history. If you want a blocker and nothing more, we are not the best-value answer, and saying otherwise would be the kind of claim this page exists to avoid.

## Not included, and why
Betfilter, Bet Breaker, Screen Stoic and Freedom all appear in other roundups. We have not verified their current pricing or tested them, so they are listed here rather than ranked — assigning them a place we hadn't checked is exactly the practice that makes these pages useless. If you have used one, tell us what it actually did.

## Platform-specific setup
Before paying for anything, check what your phone already does for free: iPhone · Android. On Android in particular, the built-in Private DNS setting blocks more than several of the paid apps here.

## The part no blocker can do
Every app on this page is one layer, and the weakest of the three that matter:
- Self-exclusion — free, and the only genuinely irreversible option. How to do it →
- A bank gambling block — free, usually with a 48-hour cooling-off before it lifts. How to turn it on →
- A blocker app — the convenience layer, and the one you can undo in a minute.

Do all three. The order above is by strength, not by ease.

## Common questions

Q: What is the best free gambling blocker?
A: BetBlocker. It is genuinely free with no ads and no upsell, run by a charity registered in Scotland (SC049565), covers Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, iOS and Fire OS, and lets you lock a self-exclusion period from one day up to five years.

Q: Is Gamban worth paying for?
A: If you gamble across a phone and a computer, yes — cross-platform coverage under one licence is what you are paying for, along with heuristic detection of new sites rather than a fixed list. If your gambling happens entirely on an iPhone, free options cover you nearly as well.

Q: Can any blocker be truly unremovable?
A: Not on iOS. Apple's sandbox does not allow an app to prevent its own deletion, so treat 'unremovable' claims about iPhones with suspicion. On Windows and Android, some blockers do resist removal much harder. The only genuinely irreversible layer on any platform is self-exclusion with the operator.

Q: Do I need a blocker if I have used GAMSTOP?
A: Yes, for a different job. GAMSTOP stops UK-licensed operators from letting you play; a blocker stops you reaching unlicensed offshore sites that GAMSTOP has no authority over. They cover each other's gaps.

Q: Should I install more than one blocker?
A: Layering different kinds helps — a DNS-level blocker plus a bank block plus self-exclusion. Installing two apps that both filter DNS mostly just creates conflicts, and on iOS only one DNS configuration can be active at a time.

# How to block gambling on Android
URL: https://trysilex.com/block-gambling-apps-android/
Language: en
Description: Android's built-in Private DNS blocks gambling in every app and browser for free, in about two minutes. Plus Digital Wellbeing, Family Link, and which third-party blockers are worth it.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Android has the best free gambling block of any phone platform and almost nobody uses it: Settings → Network & internet → Private DNS → Private DNS provider hostname, set to a filtering resolver such as family.dns.mullvad.net. That covers every app and every browser, on Wi-Fi and mobile data, in about two minutes, at no cost. Then layer Family Link (so someone else controls the settings), a bank gambling block, and self-exclusion.

Straight answer first: Silex is iPhone-only, so this page isn't selling you anything. It's the setup we'd give a friend on Android, and the free built-in option is better than most of the paid apps.

## 1. Private DNS — the two-minute one that covers everything
Android has supported encrypted DNS system-wide since Android 9. Point it at a resolver that filters gambling and those domains stop resolving in every app and every browser — sportsbook apps included — on Wi-Fi and on mobile data.
- Open Settings → Network & internet (on Samsung: Connections → More connection settings).
- Tap Private DNS.
- Choose Private DNS provider hostname.
- Enter a filtering resolver's hostname, then Save.

Resolvers that filter gambling:
Hostname | What it filters | Cost
family.dns.mullvad.net | Gambling, adult content, ads and trackers | Free, no account, published no-logging policy
<your-id>.dns.nextdns.io | Whatever you switch on — gambling is a one-tap category | Free tier, account needed, gives you logs and control

Test it. Open a browser you don't normally use and try a gambling site you actually used. It should fail to load, not just look odd. If it loads, check that a VPN isn't active — a VPN takes over DNS and silently overrides this setting.
The catch: it's a Settings toggle, so you can undo it in about a minute. That's still meaningful — most relapses are impulsive and a minute of friction stops a lot of them — but it is not a wall. Which is what the next steps are for.

## 2. Make the settings not yours to change
This is the step that turns a speed bump into something sturdier.
- Google Family Link. Put the device under supervision with a partner, parent or friend holding the supervising account. They can restrict app installs from the Play Store and control settings changes. Yes, it's built for parents; it works fine between adults who've agreed to it.
- Remove the apps and block reinstalls. Uninstall every betting app, then use Family Link's Play Store controls so reinstalling needs someone else's approval.
- Digital Wellbeing can add app timers and Focus mode. Useful for habit friction; trivially reversible, so don't count on it as a block.

## 3. Third-party blockers worth the money
App | Price | Worth it for
BetBlocker | Free, no ads, charity-run | A restriction period you set from 1 day to 5 years and cannot shorten once it starts — a real commitment device, given away
Gamban | £4.99/month or £29.99/year, 7-day trial | One subscription across Android, iOS, Windows and Mac — or its alternatives
GamBlock | Paid, pricing not published on its homepage | Claims removal "cannot happen" on Android, including blocking factory resets — the heaviest lock, if the claims hold on your device

Prices verified against each vendor's own site on 10 August 2026. Full comparison →

## 4. The two layers that aren't on your phone at all
Same on every platform, and stronger than anything above:
- Self-exclusion — free, and you can't reverse it during a craving. GAMSTOP in the UK; state programme plus each operator in the US.
- Bank gambling block — free, typically 48–72 hours to lift.

If you only have ten minutes today, do these two and come back to the phone settings afterwards.

## What doesn't work on Android
- Uninstalling the apps alone. The mobile site works, and reinstalling takes seconds.
- Router or Wi-Fi filtering by itself. Ends at your front door; mobile data walks straight past it.
- A plain VPN. Not a filter — and it can disable your Private DNS setting.
- Blocking one browser. Android will happily install another in twenty seconds.

## Then the part no blocker does
Every layer above buys you time during an urge, and urges pass in roughly 20 to 30 minutes whether or not you bet. What you do with those minutes is what decides whether this holds: riding out an urge, and the wider plan. Neither of those needs an iPhone or a subscription.

## Common questions

Q: What is the best free gambling blocker for Android?
A: Android's own Private DNS setting, pointed at a filtering resolver, blocks more than most paid apps do — every app and browser, on mobile data as well as Wi-Fi. For an app with a lockable commitment period, BetBlocker is free, charity-run, and supports Android.

Q: Does Private DNS work on mobile data?
A: Yes. That's what makes it better than router-level or Wi-Fi-only blocking, which stops working the moment the phone leaves the house. Private DNS is a device setting and applies everywhere.

Q: Can I stop myself turning Private DNS off?
A: Not by itself — it's a Settings toggle, so it's a speed bump rather than a wall. To make it stick, put the device under Family Link with someone else holding the account, or use a blocker that resists removal. And rely on the layers you can't undo at all: self-exclusion and a bank block.

Q: Does Silex work on Android?
A: No. Silex is iPhone-only, and there's no Android version planned in the near term. If you're on Android, the setup on this page plus BetBlocker or Gamban is what we'd genuinely recommend — we'd rather tell you that than waste your time.

Q: Will a VPN block gambling sites on Android?
A: A standard VPN, no — it moves where your traffic exits, it doesn't filter it. Some privacy VPNs include a content-filtering DNS mode that does block gambling categories. Note that an active VPN can override your Private DNS setting, which is a common reason blocking silently stops working.

# How to block gambling sites and apps on iPhone
URL: https://trysilex.com/block-gambling-sites-iphone/
Language: en
Description: Every working method for blocking gambling on an iPhone — Screen Time, a system-wide DNS profile, Safari content blockers, bank blocks and self-exclusion — with what each one actually covers and how easily you can undo it.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Screen Time alone won't do it. The combination that holds is: a system-wide DNS profile (covers every app and browser), Screen Time restrictions with the passcode held by someone else (stops reinstalling), and the two layers you cannot undo in a craving — operator self-exclusion and a bank gambling block. Setting up all four takes about 30 minutes.

On Android instead? Here's the Android setup — the free built-in option there is genuinely better.
There are five distinct ways to block gambling on an iPhone, and they cover different things. Most guides list one, that one has a hole in it, and the hole is where the relapse goes. Here is all of it, with the honest limitations of each.

## Start here: what each method actually covers
Method | Covers | How fast can you undo it? | Cost
Screen Time restrictions | App installs, named websites in Safari, app hiding | Seconds — unless someone else holds the passcode | Free
System-wide DNS profile | Every app and every browser, on Wi-Fi and cellular | About a minute, in Settings | Free options exist
Safari content blocker | Safari only | Seconds | Free or bundled with an app
Bank gambling block | Card payments to gambling merchants | Often a 48-hour cooling-off before it lifts | Free
Operator self-exclusion | Your accounts, at the source | You can't — months to years | Free

Read that table as a stack, not a menu. The first three make gambling inconvenient; the last two make it genuinely hard. People who only do the first three tend to relapse through a browser or a payment method they forgot about.

## 1. Screen Time: block installs and named sites
Screen Time is free, built in, and more useful for what it prevents than for what it filters.
Stop new gambling apps appearing: Settings → Screen Time → Content & Privacy Restrictions → turn on → iTunes & App Store Purchases → Installing Apps → Don't Allow. This is the highest-value switch on the whole phone. Delete the sportsbook apps first, then flip it — now reinstalling requires the Screen Time passcode.
Block gambling websites in Safari: Content & Privacy Restrictions → Content Restrictions → Web Content → Limit Adult Websites, then add each operator under Never Allow. Turning on Limit Adult Websites also disables Private Browsing in Safari, which is a genuine bonus.
The catch nobody mentions: iOS has no gambling category. "Limit Adult Websites" is an adult-content filter; it catches some gambling sites incidentally and misses most sportsbooks. If you rely on it alone you will be blocked from nothing you actually use. The Never Allow list works, but you are maintaining it by hand against an industry with thousands of mirror domains.
Do this bit properly: set a Screen Time passcode you don't know. Have your partner, a friend, or a family member type it in and keep it. Everything above is a five-second undo for whoever holds that code — so make sure that isn't you at 1am.

## 2. A system-wide DNS profile: the one that covers everything
This is the method most guides skip, and it is the strongest thing that lives on the phone itself. Every app and browser has to look up a domain name before it can connect. If the lookup fails, the app fails — no extension needed, no per-browser setup, and it works on cellular data as well as Wi-Fi.
iOS lets an app or a configuration profile install an encrypted-DNS (DoH) setting that applies device-wide. Point it at a resolver that filters gambling and every sportsbook, casino and slots site stops resolving.
Free and paid options that filter gambling:
- Mullvad's public DoH resolvers — a free "family" resolver that blocks gambling among other categories, run under a published no-logging policy.
- NextDNS — free tier for moderate query volumes, with a gambling blocklist you switch on plus a large catalogue of community lists.
- Control D — similar idea, category filtering, free tier available.
- A blocker app that installs the profile for you — including Silex, which sets up an encrypted-DNS shield and merges public gambling-domain lists so you never maintain one by hand.

Verify it after setup: Settings → General → VPN, DNS & Device Management → DNS should show your chosen configuration as selected, and a known gambling site should fail to load in a browser you don't normally use.
Its limitation, stated plainly: you can turn it off in Settings in under a minute. DNS filtering is a speed bump against a determined craving, not a wall. It is an excellent speed bump — most relapses are impulsive, and one minute of friction is often enough — but do not treat it as the last line.

## 3. Safari content blockers
A content blocker extension can refuse to load a list of domains inside Safari. Enable one at Settings → Apps → Safari → Extensions, then switch the blocker on. Silex ships one; so do most dedicated blocker apps.
Useful, and narrow: it covers Safari and nothing else. Chrome, Firefox, Edge, the in-app browser inside a social app and the sportsbook's own native app are all untouched. Treat a Safari blocker as a supplement to DNS filtering, never a replacement.

## 4. Make your bank decline the payment
Blocking access is only half of it — the other half is making the money hard to move. Most UK banks and a growing number of US and Canadian ones offer a gambling-merchant block that declines transactions to gambling operators outright, and many enforce a cooling-off period (often 48 hours) before they will lift it.
That cooling-off is the point: it makes the block outlast the urge. Here's how to turn it on, bank by bank.

## 5. Self-exclude at the source
The strongest layer isn't on your phone at all. Self-exclusion means telling the operator, or a national scheme, to close your accounts and refuse you service for a fixed period. In the UK, GAMSTOP covers every UK-licensed online operator with one free registration. In the US, most states run self-exclusion programmes, and every licensed sportsbook has its own.
You cannot undo this in a craving — that is precisely why it works. The full self-exclusion guide is here.

## What doesn't work
- Just deleting the apps. Reinstalling takes fifteen seconds, and the mobile website works fine without any app at all.
- Router-level blocking on its own. Home Wi-Fi filtering, including a Pi-hole or a router-level DNS change, evaporates the moment the phone switches to cellular. Do it as well, never instead.
- A general VPN. It relocates your traffic; it doesn't filter it. Some privacy VPNs offer a content-filtering DNS mode, which does work — the plain VPN does nothing for you here.
- An app whose only feature is a streak counter. Tracking is a motivator, not a barrier. You need both, and the barrier goes in first.
- Anything that promises to be unremovable on iOS. The sandbox does not permit it. Claims like that are marketing, and believing them is how people end up with one layer instead of four.

## The 30-minute setup, in order
- Delete every gambling app. Sign out of any operator accounts still logged in on the browser.
- Turn on a filtering DNS profile, and confirm a gambling site fails to load.
- Screen Time → Installing Apps → Don't Allow, plus Never Allow entries for the sites you actually used. Hand the passcode to someone else.
- Enable a Safari content blocker.
- Call or message your bank and ask for the gambling block.
- Self-exclude with every operator you have an account with — and with GAMSTOP if you are in the UK.

Steps 5 and 6 are the ones people postpone, and they are the ones that hold. Do them first if you only have ten minutes.

## Blocking is the floor, not the plan
Every layer above buys you time in the ninety seconds when an urge peaks. What you do with that time decides whether it works twice. Urges rise, crest and fall on a fairly predictable curve, and learning to wait one out is a skill that improves with repetition. That is what the 90-day side of this is for.

## Common questions

Q: Can I block gambling apps on iPhone without an app?
A: Yes. Screen Time can block the App Store and specific websites, and iOS can install a DNS configuration that makes gambling domains fail to resolve in every app. Both are free and built in. What iOS cannot do on its own is maintain the list of hundreds of thousands of gambling domains — that is what a blocker app or a filtering DNS service adds.

Q: Does Screen Time block gambling apps?
A: Partly. Screen Time can stop new apps being installed, hide apps you have, and block specific websites in Safari. It has no gambling category, so 'Limit Adult Websites' is not a gambling filter — you have to add domains to Never Allow yourself, or use a filtering DNS resolver that keeps the list for you.

Q: Can gambling apps be blocked permanently on iPhone?
A: No, and any app claiming otherwise is overselling. On iOS you can always remove a profile or delete an app. Permanence has to come from outside the phone: self-exclusion with the operator, and a block at your bank. Those two you genuinely cannot reverse in the ninety seconds a craving lasts.

Q: Will a VPN block gambling sites?
A: A general-purpose VPN will not — it changes where your traffic exits, not what it can reach. A filtering DNS service or DNS-based blocker is what you want. Some privacy VPNs bundle a content-filtering DNS option, which does work.

Q: Does blocking work on cellular data as well as Wi-Fi?
A: A DNS configuration installed on the iPhone does, because it belongs to the device. Router-level blocking does not — it stops at your front door, and the phone falls straight back to gambling as soon as it switches to 5G. This is the single most common reason home blocking fails.

========================================================================
# How to make your bank decline gambling payments
URL: https://trysilex.com/block-gambling-transactions-bank/
Language: en
Description: Bank gambling blocks decline payments to betting operators and take days to lift. Which UK banks offer one, what US cardholders can do instead, and why the cooling-off period is the whole point.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Most major UK banks let you switch on a gambling block in the app, and it takes a 48 to 72-hour cooling-off period to switch back off — which is exactly why it works. In the US there is no consumer toggle at most banks, but gambling deposits on credit cards are already widely declined under merchant category code 7995, and you can ask your issuer to block that code.

Blocking websites stops you reaching the bet. Blocking payments stops you funding it, and it is the harder of the two to undo — which makes it the more valuable one. A gambling block at your bank refuses transactions to gambling merchants outright, and reversing it takes days rather than seconds.

## Why the delay is the feature
Every layer worth having is really a bet on time. Gambling urges are impulsive and short-lived; a barrier that takes one minute to remove often fails, and a barrier that takes two days almost never does. When a bank makes you wait 48 hours to re-enable gambling payments, it has converted a decision made in the worst possible state of mind into one made two days later, calm.
The research on card blockers makes the same point about design details — the University of Bristol's Personal Finance Research Centre published a blueprint for bank card gambling blockers arguing that friction to unblock matters as much as the block itself.

## UK: turn it on in the app
Most UK current accounts now include a gambling block, usually under card controls or spending limits in the mobile app. Reported behaviour, which you should confirm with your own bank because these terms change:
Bank | Reported cooling-off to lift
Monzo | You choose: 2 days up to 12 months, and you must wait it out
Starling | 48 hours
Lloyds (and Halifax, Bank of Scotland) | 48 hours
NatWest (and RBS) | 48 hours, lifted via the app
Barclays | 72 hours
HSBC | Cooling-off period applies
Santander | Block available

If your bank isn't listed, phone them and ask directly for a gambling transaction block — coverage across UK banks and building societies is now wide, and the frontline staff at most of them handle this request routinely and without any awkwardness. GamCare maintains a plain-language explainer of how bank gambling blocks work.
Pick the longest period you can stand. Monzo's up-to-12-months option is the strongest single money-side commitment available from a UK bank, and it is free.

## US: what actually exists
There is no widely available "block gambling" switch in US banking apps. What exists instead:
- Credit cards mostly already decline it. Online gambling merchants are assigned merchant category code 7995, and major US issuers treat gambling deposits as cash advances or cash equivalents — several blanket-decline the code. If you have been funding gambling by credit card, this may already be closing.
- Ask your issuer to block MCC 7995 permanently. Say exactly that: "please place a permanent block on merchant category code 7995 on my account." Some banks will do it, some will tell you it is already in place, and a few will say they can't — in which case ask for the request to be noted.
- Remove the cards from the operator's side. Delete saved cards and bank links from every sportsbook and casino account you have. Do it in the same sitting as self-exclusion, because self-exclusion closes the account that holds them.
- Watch the e-wallet gap. PayPal, Venmo, Cash App, prepaid cards and crypto on-ramps are the usual detour when a card stops working. Closing or unlinking those matters as much as the card block.

## What a bank block does not cover
- Miscategorised merchants. The block reads the merchant's category code. Operators occasionally sit under a code that doesn't trip it.
- Intermediaries. A payment to an e-wallet is a payment to an e-wallet as far as your bank is concerned, whatever happens next.
- Cash, and other people's money. No bank control reaches an ATM withdrawal, a friend's card, or borrowing.
- Another account. Blocking one bank while holding an unblocked account somewhere else does very little. Block them all, including the one you barely use.

## Do these three in one sitting
- The bank block — on every account and card you hold, not just the main one.
- Self-exclusion — which closes the accounts your cards are saved in.
- Phone-level blocking — so the sites stop loading in the first place.

Twenty minutes, no cost, and between them they remove almost every route that a craving takes when it is looking for one. Then comes the part that actually decides the outcome — what you do with the urge once the door is shut. That's here.

## If gambling has left debt behind
Blocking payments doesn't address money already owed, and debt pressure is one of the most reliable triggers for chasing losses. Free, non-judgemental advice: StepChange and National Debtline in the UK, NFCC member agencies in the US. None of them charge, and talking to one is not a commitment to anything.

## Common questions

Q: Which UK banks have a gambling block?
A: Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Santander, Monzo and Starling all offer one, along with several others. Reported cooling-off periods before the block can be lifted range from 48 hours (Starling, Lloyds, NatWest) to 72 hours (Barclays), and Monzo lets you set anything from 2 days to 12 months. Confirm the current terms with your own bank — they change.

Q: Does a gambling block stop every gambling payment?
A: No. It works on the merchant category the operator is registered under, so a payment routed through an e-wallet, a crypto exchange or a merchant miscategorised as something else can slip past. It also does not stop cash. Treat it as a strong layer, not a seal.

Q: Can I block gambling on a US bank card?
A: Rarely as a self-service switch. But gambling deposits on US credit cards are commonly declined already — issuers treat them as cash advances or cash equivalents and many blanket-decline merchant code 7995. Call your issuer and ask for a permanent block on that code; some will set it, and some will simply confirm it is already in place.

Q: Will the block affect anything else?
A: Occasionally. Merchant categorisation is imperfect, so a small number of legitimate payments — a lottery-adjacent retailer, an arcade, some prize-draw sites — can be caught. That is a minor inconvenience against the thing it prevents.

Q: Is a bank block better than a blocker app?
A: It is stronger, because you cannot lift it in the ninety seconds an urge lasts. It is also narrower, because it only touches money movement, not access. Use both.

# Gamban alternatives
URL: https://trysilex.com/gamban-alternatives/
Language: en
Description: Gamban costs £4.99 a month or £29.99 a year. Here are the free and paid alternatives that cover the same job, what each does better, and when Gamban is still the right answer.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Gamban is £4.99/month or £29.99/year with a 7-day free trial, covering iOS, Android, Windows and Mac. If you want free, BetBlocker (charity-run) does the core job on more platforms than Gamban. If you want the strongest removal resistance on Windows or Android, look at GamBlock. If you want a quit program rather than just a wall, Silex — which we make — is iPhone-only and costs more. And if you only gamble on an iPhone, iOS's own DNS and Screen Time settings plus a free filtering resolver cost nothing at all.

Disclosure: we make Silex, one of the options below. So this page verifies every price against the vendor's own site rather than repeating other comparisons, and it says where Gamban beats us. Prices checked 10 August 2026.

## What you're actually replacing
Gamban's pricing page lists £4.99 billed monthly or £29.99 billed annually (advertised as saving 49%), with a 7-day free trial and no payment required up front. One subscription covers iOS, Android, Windows and Mac, and the plans include blocking, progress monitoring, layered self-exclusion and on-demand technical support.
People usually look for an alternative for one of four reasons: they want it free, they only need one platform, they want something harder to remove, or blocking alone hasn't been enough.

## The alternatives
Option | Price | Platforms | Better than Gamban at

### BetBlocker — the free one that isn't a downgrade
A charity project (founded by ThePOGG in 2017, independent charity from 2019, registered in Scotland SC049565). Free "absolutely nothing. Ever.", ad-free, and it states coverage of 356,000+ websites and 1,900+ apps with 105,000+ active users. Its standout feature is a restriction period you set from one day to five years and cannot shorten once running.
Where Gamban wins: polish, support, and heuristic detection of sites that aren't on a list yet. BetBlocker's setup is more manual. betblocker.org

### GamBlock — for a Windows problem
Uses heuristics rather than lists — "GamBlock uses heuristics to ban gambling sites rather than the simple lists imitators use that are never up to date" — and on Windows and Android claims removal "cannot happen", including blocking attempts to reset the machine.
Where Gamban wins: published pricing and a much easier purchase decision. We haven't independently tested GamBlock's removal-resistance claims, so treat them as the vendor's until you've tried them in a refund window. gamblock.com

### NextDNS or Control D — the technical route
Not blocker apps but filtering DNS services with gambling categories you switch on. Set one as the DNS on your iPhone and it covers every app and browser on cellular and Wi-Fi; set it on your router and it covers the house. Free tiers are enough for one person, and this is what most blocker apps are doing under the hood anyway.
Where Gamban wins: you have to be comfortable with profiles and DNS settings, and nothing stops you switching the profile off — there's no commitment mechanism at all.

### Silex — different product, not a cheaper Gamban
iPhone only, $4.99/week or $49.99/year with a 3-day trial. It installs an encrypted-DNS shield covering every app and browser, ships a Safari content blocker, and guides setup of the layers software can't provide — self-exclusion, bank blocks, killing promo emails.
The reason to choose it is the other half: a 90-day program written from clinical CBT material, an urge button that is never paywalled, and a running total of the money you kept.
Where Gamban wins, clearly: platforms. Gamban covers your laptop; Silex does not exist on anything but an iPhone. Gamban is also cheaper annually, and has years of operating history where we have weeks. If what you need is a blocker, Gamban or BetBlocker is the better buy and we'd rather say so than sell you the wrong thing.

## When you should just keep Gamban
- You gamble on more than one kind of device.
- You want one subscription, one support contact, and no assembly.
- It's already installed and working — swapping tools is a common form of procrastination that feels like progress.

## The change that matters more than which app you pick
Every option on this page is the same layer, and it's the weakest of the three. Before spending another hour comparing blockers, spend twenty minutes on the two free things no app can do for you:
- Self-exclude — GAMSTOP in the UK, your state programme and each operator in the US. Free, and you can't reverse it in a craving.
- Bank gambling block — free, and typically 48 to 72 hours to lift.

Then pick whichever blocker you'll actually keep installed. Full comparison of all of them →

## Common questions

Q: How much does Gamban cost?
A: £4.99 billed monthly, or £29.99 billed annually, with a 7-day free trial and no payment up front. Checked against gamban.com/pricing on 10 August 2026. Older roundups still quoting £24.99 a year are out of date.

Q: Is there a free alternative to Gamban?
A: Yes — BetBlocker, run by a charity registered in Scotland (SC049565). It is free with no ads, states it blocks 356,000+ gambling sites and 1,900+ apps, and supports Windows, Mac, Linux, Android, iOS and Fire OS. It also lets you lock a restriction period of up to five years.

Q: Can I cancel Gamban if it stops working for me?
A: It's an ordinary subscription, cancelled through wherever you bought it. Worth knowing: cancelling a blocker is by design easy, which is why it should never be your only layer — self-exclusion and a bank block are the ones that hold.

Q: Is Gamban better than GAMSTOP?
A: They do different jobs and you want both. GAMSTOP stops UK-licensed operators from serving you; Gamban blocks access to gambling sites generally, including the unlicensed offshore ones GAMSTOP has no authority over.

Q: Does Gamban work on iPhone?
A: Yes, and like every iOS blocker it can be removed from Settings — Apple's sandbox does not permit an app to make itself undeletable. That is a platform limit, not a Gamban flaw.

# Gambling debt: where to start
URL: https://trysilex.com/gambling-debt-help/
Language: en
Description: How to deal with debt from gambling — stop the bleeding, work out what's actually owed, get free charity debt advice, and avoid the consolidation traps aimed at people in exactly this position.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: In order: stop new losses (self-exclusion and a bank block, both free and both today), write down every debt in one place including the money owed to people, then call a free debt charity — StepChange or National Debtline in the UK, an NFCC member agency in the US. They are free, they don't judge, and they get better outcomes than anything you can arrange alone at 2am. Do not take a consolidation loan while you are still gambling.

Gambling debt has one feature that makes it different from ordinary debt: the thing that caused it looks, from the inside, like the fastest way to fix it. That belief is what turns a manageable number into an unmanageable one, and it is the first thing to disarm.

## 1. Stop the bleeding before you do the arithmetic
There's no point building a repayment plan around a balance that's still moving. Both of these are free and take under twenty minutes:
- Self-exclude from every operator — GAMSTOP covers all UK-licensed sites in one registration; in the US, your state programme plus each sportsbook.
- Bank gambling block — declines payments to gambling merchants and takes 48–72 hours to lift.

Then block it on your phone. In that order: strongest first.

## 2. Get all of it onto one page
Most people carrying gambling debt have never seen the full number, because it's spread across cards, overdrafts, an app loan, a payday lender and three people they can't face. The fragmentation is doing you harm — it makes the total feel survivable in a way that keeps you from acting.
Write down, for each one: who it's owed to, how much, the interest rate, the minimum payment. Include money owed to family and friends, even though it has no paperwork. Include anything borrowed against your salary.
Then separate them. Debts where the consequence is losing your home, your utilities, your transport to work or your liberty come first — in UK debt advice these are called priority debts, and they get dealt with ahead of credit cards regardless of who is shouting loudest. A debt adviser will do this triage with you in one call, and it is the part people most often get wrong alone.

## 3. Call a free debt charity
This is the highest-value phone call available to you, and the thing people delay for months out of shame.
- UK: StepChange and National Debtline. Free, charity-run, no judgement, and they'll talk to creditors for you.
- US: NFCC member agencies — non-profit credit counselling, free initial counselling.
- Either: the national gambling helplines will point you at local debt help as part of the same call. US 1-800-GAMBLER, UK 0808 8020 133.

What they can arrange that you generally can't alone: frozen interest, paused collection, affordable repayment plans, and — in England and Wales — the Breathing Space scheme, which stops most interest, fees and enforcement action for 60 days while you get advice. Ask whether you qualify.

## 4. What to avoid
- Consolidation while you're still gambling. It converts several maxed balances into one loan plus several empty credit lines. This is how a £10,000 problem becomes a £25,000 one, and it happens to people who were genuinely trying to fix it.
- Anyone charging a fee to "sort" gambling debt. Free charities do the same work better. Paid debt-relief outfits target this exact search.
- Borrowing from family to clear it in one go. If you're still gambling, it reloads rather than resolves — and it converts a financial problem into a relationship one. (It's also why families are advised not to clear gambling debts. If someone has said no to you, that's why — it isn't abandonment.)
- Any plan that requires a win. Including "one last session to get back to level". This is the belief that built the debt, wearing a suit.
- Crypto, high-risk trading, or a "system". Same loop, different interface.

## 5. Expect the debt itself to be a trigger
This is the part standard debt advice misses. Statements, calls and the size of the number produce exactly the stress state that used to be answered with a bet — which is why the blocks in step 1 need to be up before you start opening envelopes.
Two things help: a repayment plan you didn't design alone, so the number stops being an emergency and becomes a schedule; and knowing that the urge to fix it in one night peaks and passes like any other. Usually in 20 to 30 minutes.

## 6. Watch the number move the other way
Once the losses stop, the money you're not gambling starts doing something. Seeing that as a rising figure rather than an absence is a surprisingly durable motivator — it's why Silex counts the money you kept instead of the days you white-knuckled. Work out what a year of not gambling is worth to you →

## If the debt has you thinking about not being here
Gambling debt and suicidal thoughts are strongly linked, and financial shame is a particularly isolating kind. Please use the numbers below — in the US, 988; in the UK, Samaritans on 116 123. Debt is solvable, including debt that currently looks unsolvable, and free advisers deal with worse numbers than yours every day of the week.

## Common questions

Q: Can I get help with gambling debt for free?
A: Yes, and free help is better than paid help here. StepChange and National Debtline in the UK, and NFCC member agencies in the US, are non-profit, charge nothing, and will negotiate with creditors on your behalf. Anyone charging you a fee upfront to fix gambling debt is selling you something you can get for nothing.

Q: Should I take a loan to pay off gambling debt?
A: Not while you are still gambling — a consolidation loan clears balances that then become fresh credit lines, which is the single most common way gambling debt doubles. Once you have genuinely stopped and the blocks are in place, a debt adviser can tell you whether consolidation makes sense for your particular situation. That is their job, and they have no product to sell you.

Q: Will creditors know it was gambling?
A: You don't have to itemise the cause, but telling a debt adviser is worth it — they'll factor it in, and many lenders have vulnerability policies that can mean frozen interest or paused collection. In England and Wales, a debt adviser can also tell you whether you qualify for the Breathing Space scheme, which pauses most interest and enforcement for 60 days.

Q: Should I tell my family about the debt?
A: Almost always, and sooner is easier than later — the number only grows while it's secret, and secrecy is the thing that makes gambling debt escalate. It's worth speaking to a helpline first to plan how, especially if housing or children are involved.

Q: Does bankruptcy clear gambling debt?
A: In many places gambling debts are treated like other unsecured debts in insolvency, but the rules, the consequences and the alternatives differ a lot by country and by situation, and there are usually less drastic options. This is exactly the decision to take to a free debt adviser rather than to a forum.

# Gambling loss calculator
URL: https://trysilex.com/gambling-loss-calculator/
Language: en
Description: Put in what you lose in a typical week and see the yearly, 5-year and 10-year total, plus what the same money would have compounded to. Runs in your browser; nothing is stored.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Enter what you lose in a typical week. The yearly figure is that number × 52; the long-run figures add compounding for scale. Most people are shocked less by the weekly number than by the ten-year one. Nothing you type is stored or sent.

## Why the ten-year number is the one that lands
A £60 weekend feels like the price of entertainment. Ten years of £60 weekends is a deposit on a flat. Nothing about the arithmetic is surprising — what's surprising is that almost nobody does it, because gambling losses arrive in small pieces and never appear on a single statement line.
This is also why the money figure works as a recovery tool rather than a guilt trip. Silex takes the same weekly number and counts upward from the day you stop, so the sum you'd have lost becomes the sum you kept. Same arithmetic, opposite direction.

## What the number does not include
- Borrowing. Interest on money borrowed to gamble often costs more than the losses themselves. The PGSI asks about borrowing for a reason — it's one of the strongest markers of a heavy pattern.
- Time. Hours in an app at 1am don't show up in a currency figure and are frequently the loss people most regret.
- The near-misses that kept you in. Losses disguised as wins — a return smaller than your stake, presented with celebration sound and colour — are a designed feature of modern slots and betting apps, not an accident. The research on that is worth reading.

## If the figure is worse than you expected
That reaction is information, not a verdict. Two next steps, in this order:
- Take the 9-question PGSI self-check — it takes two minutes and tells you where the pattern sits.
- Put blocks between you and the operators, starting with your phone, then the two that don't rely on willpower: self-exclusion and a bank gambling block.

If gambling has left debt behind, deal with that alongside — free, non-judgemental debt advice is available from StepChange and National Debtline in the UK, and from NFCC member agencies in the US. None of them charge, and none of them will lecture you.

## Common questions

Q: Should I use my losses or my total stakes?
A: Use net losses — money gone, not money wagered. Total stakes are usually far higher than losses because winnings get re-bet, and counting them makes the figure look dramatic but meaningless.

Q: I don't know what I lose in a week. How do I find out?
A: Take the last three months of bank or card statements and add every transfer to a gambling operator, then subtract every withdrawal from one. Divide by 13. Card statements catch what memory doesn't — most people underestimate by a wide margin.

Q: Why include an investment comparison at all?
A: Because the honest cost of gambling isn't only the money lost, it's what that money would have become. The figure uses an 8% average annual return compounded monthly, which is an illustration for scale — not a forecast, not a recommendation, and not financial advice.

Q: Does the number include what I owe?
A: No. This calculates ongoing losses only. If gambling has left you with debt, a free debt-advice charity is a better next call than a calculator — StepChange or National Debtline in the UK, an NFCC member agency in the US.

# What happens when you stop gambling
URL: https://trysilex.com/gambling-recovery-timeline/
Language: en
Description: Withdrawal, sleep, mood, money and the danger points — what the first 90 days after quitting gambling commonly look like, and which weeks people actually relapse in.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: The first 72 hours are usually the loudest: irritability, poor sleep, and urges arriving in clusters. Weeks 1–2 are peak frequency. Around weeks 3–6 comes the quiet danger zone — the urges have eased, the crisis feeling has passed, and "maybe I could handle a small one" shows up. By 90 days most people report urges that are occasional and manageable rather than absent. Cue-triggered flickers years later are normal and don't mean it failed.

Nobody tells you what the first month feels like, so it's easy to read a bad week as evidence that quitting isn't working — when a bad week is exactly what the process looks like. Here's the shape most people describe.
This is a composite of commonly reported patterns and of relapse-prevention research, not a clinical prediction. Yours will be lumpier than any timeline, and that's normal.

## Days 1–3: the loud part
Urges arrive often, and in clusters that feel like one long craving. Irritability, restlessness and broken sleep are common, as are headaches and appetite changes. Gambling isn't a substance, so there's no detox — but the discomfort is genuinely physical for a lot of people, and being told "it's just psychological" helps nobody.
Two things belong in these 72 hours. Get the barriers up while motivation is at its highest — self-exclusion, bank block, phone blocking. And tell one person. Both get harder to do on day nine than on day one.

## Week 1–2: peak frequency
Urges are at their most frequent here, and each one still peaks and passes in roughly 20 to 30 minutes. That pattern is the thing to lean on.
What else shows up:
- Sleep starts improving, often the first visible win — the late-night sessions were costing more than money.
- The time is suddenly obvious. Evenings feel long and empty. This is the vacancy gambling used to fill, and it needs an occupant.
- The money arrives as a shock. Both directions: what's still owed, and what's no longer leaving.
- Predictable spikes: payday, a big fixture, your old time slot.

## Weeks 3–6: the quiet danger zone
This is the part worth marking in advance, because it's the window that catches people who got through week one fine.
By now the urges have eased, sleep is better, the emergency feeling has passed — and precisely because things are better, a new thought becomes persuasive: maybe it wasn't that bad. Maybe I could have one small bet now that I'm in control.
That thought is the single most reliable predictor of a relapse at this stage, and it arrives wearing the clothes of recovery rather than of craving. It is also why blocks you set up in week one need to be ones you can't casually undo in week four — which is the entire argument for self-exclusion over an app you can delete.

## Weeks 6–12: it starts becoming ordinary
- Urges become occasional and cue-linked rather than ambient.
- Mood generally lifts — later than sleep did. If it hasn't by now, see a doctor; depression and anxiety travel alongside gambling problems often enough that waiting it out is the wrong call.
- Money becomes a plan instead of a panic, especially if you've spoken to a free debt adviser.
- The replacement matters more than the resistance now. Whatever gambling was doing — escape, action, company — has to have somewhere else to go. That's step three of the plan.

## Past 90 days
Most people describe this as maintenance rather than survival. What persists is cue-triggered flickers — walking past a shop, a big final, a bonus landing — and they're usually brief and easy to dismiss. That's not failure or a sign it's coming back. It just means a cue is still a cue.
What tends to hold up long-term: the irreversible blocks staying in place, at least one person who knows, and a life with enough in it that gambling would have to displace something you'd miss.

## If you slip somewhere in here
Common, and not a reset. What decides the outcome is what happens in the following hour, not the bet itself — the first-hour plan is here. Silex is built on the same principle: a lapse routes you to a Reset day, and your history is never wiped.

## Why Silex is 90 days
Not arbitrary, and not a claim about your brain finishing on a particular date. Roughly three months is how long it commonly takes for urges to thin out and for something else to occupy the space — and a day-by-day structure exists mostly to get you through weeks 3 to 6, when nothing feels urgent and quitting quietly stops being a project. What the program is built from →

## Common questions

Q: Is there physical withdrawal from gambling?
A: Gambling disorder is a behavioural addiction, so there's no medical detox — but plenty of people report genuinely physical symptoms in the first days: disturbed sleep, restlessness, irritability, headaches, low mood and appetite changes. It's real, and it's short.

Q: When is relapse most likely?
A: Two windows. The first week, when urges are most frequent and the blocks may not be set up yet. And weeks 3 to 6, when things have improved enough that the problem feels solved — which is when the idea of a controlled, small bet becomes persuasive. The second window catches more people, because the first one is the one everyone prepares for.

Q: How long until I stop thinking about gambling?
A: Frequency usually drops sharply after the first fortnight and keeps easing over about three months. "Not thinking about it at all" tends to arrive later than "not acting on it", and most people find the thoughts get quieter and less urgent rather than vanishing on a particular day.

Q: Will my sleep and mood go back to normal?
A: For most people, yes, and sleep is often the first visible improvement — commonly within the first two weeks once late-night sessions stop. Mood typically lags behind sleep. If low mood persists well beyond the first month, that's worth taking to a doctor rather than waiting out, as depression and anxiety commonly travel alongside gambling problems.

Q: Does the 90-day figure mean anything?
A: It's a useful frame rather than a biological deadline. Roughly three months is how long it commonly takes for urges to thin out and for something else to have taken gambling's place in your week. Nothing switches off at day 90 — but by then most people are doing maintenance rather than survival.

========================================================================
# I gambled again — what to do now
URL: https://trysilex.com/gambling-relapse/
Language: en
Description: A slip is not the end of quitting — how you interpret it decides what happens next. The abstinence violation effect, the practical first hour after a lapse, and how to turn it into information.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Stop the session now, not after one more bet. Then, in this order: put the money out of reach, tell one person, and write down what happened before the first bet. What turns a slip into a full relapse is almost never the slip — it is the conclusion "I've blown it, so I may as well finish the job." That reaction has a name in the research: the abstinence violation effect.

If you have just gambled and you are still in the session, close it. Not after one more, not after you have got back to even. Now. Everything else on this page can wait ten minutes; that can't.

## The next hour, in order
- Put the money out of reach. Log out. Delete the app. Turn on your bank's gambling block — most take 48 hours to lift, which is exactly the delay you need. If you have someone you trust, hand them your card for the night. Do this before you feel calmer, not after.
- Eat something and drink water. This sounds absurd on a page about addiction. It isn't: a lot of the desperation in the hour after a loss is a physical state, and it lifts measurably with food, water and sleep.
- Tell one person. Someone who knows you are trying to stop, or a free helpline — the numbers below are answered 24/7 by people who take exactly this call all day and will not be shocked. Saying it out loud is what stops it becoming a secret, and secrecy is what lets a slip grow into a month. (If you're dreading their reaction, it may help to know what the people around you are advised to do — it is less punitive than you're imagining.)
- Don't make any financial decisions tonight. No loan applications, no asking for an advance, no moving money between accounts, no decisions about telling your employer. All of it is better in daylight, and none of it is better at 2am.
- Write down what happened before the first bet. Where you were, what time it was, what you felt, what you had just seen. Not to punish yourself — this is the single most valuable piece of information you will get this month, and it is only available for a few hours before memory smooths it out.

## Why the slip usually isn't the problem
Relapse-prevention research made a distinction that changed how this is treated: a lapse is a single instance, a relapse is a full return to the old pattern, and the bridge between them is mostly interpretation.
Marlatt and Gordon named the mechanism the abstinence violation effect: after breaking a self-imposed rule, people often feel guilt and a collapse of self-belief — "I've proven I can't do this" — and that reaction is what drives the second, third and tenth bet. The same person, same slip, reaching for "well, that told me something useful about Fridays" instead of "I'm hopeless", is in a completely different position.
This is not positive thinking. It is that shame is a poor motivator and an excellent concealer, and concealment is how gambling problems escalate.

## Turn it into information
Once the immediate risk is handled, get specific. Most lapses have a traceable chain, and the useful link is usually two or three steps before the bet:
Ask | Why it matters
What was the first moment I could have stopped this? | Almost always earlier than the bet — opening the app "just to look", checking odds, reading a promo email.
Which layer failed, and why? | Was the block off? Did you find an unblocked route? Did the money come from somewhere you hadn't covered?
What was I feeling twenty minutes before? | Bored, angry, lonely, hopeful, celebrating. The emotional trigger repeats far more reliably than the situation does.
What did I tell myself to make it OK? | "Just a small one." "I'm owed a win." "One last time before I stop properly." Learning your own scripts is how you catch the next one mid-sentence.

Then close the specific gap. A slip through a browser you forgot means adding device-wide DNS blocking. A slip funded by an e-wallet means closing the e-wallet. A slip on an unlicensed site means self-exclusion won't cover it and a blocker has to.

## What not to do
- Don't chase. Trying to win it back is the phase where most of the real damage happens, and it is one of the PGSI's nine screening items for a reason.
- Don't reset your counter to zero and treat the whole thing as void. The days before the slip happened. You learned things in them. They count.
- Don't quit quitting until Monday. "I'll start again properly next week" is the most expensive sentence in this whole subject.
- Don't borrow to cover it. If money is now short, talk to a free debt charity before a lender: StepChange or National Debtline in the UK, NFCC members in the US.

## How Silex handles it
Because it's the design question that matters most in an app like this: a lapse in Silex doesn't wipe anything. It routes you to a Reset day — a lesson built around the questions above — and your history and earned milestones stay exactly where they were. There is one milestone piece you can only earn by completing a Reset day after a lapse, because repairing something is a skill worth rewarding rather than a failure worth marking.

## If tonight is worse than a bad night
Gambling losses and thoughts of suicide travel together more often than most people realise. If your thoughts have gone there, please use one of the numbers below now — they are free, confidential, and you do not have to be in crisis to call one.

## Common questions

Q: Does a slip mean I have to start over?
A: Only if you decide to score it that way. You have not lost the weeks of learning, the blocks you set up, or the reasons you stopped. Any system that zeroes your progress after one lapse is teaching you to hide the next one, which is the opposite of what you need.

Q: What is the abstinence violation effect?
A: A finding from relapse-prevention research (Marlatt and Gordon): after breaking a rule they set themselves, people commonly experience guilt and a sense of lost control, and that reaction — rather than the lapse itself — drives the return to full use. How you interpret the slip predicts the outcome better than the slip does.

Q: Should I tell my partner I gambled again?
A: Almost always yes, and sooner is easier than later. Secrecy is the mechanism that lets a relapse grow, and the conversation you are dreading is smaller today than it will be after three more weeks of hiding it. If safety or housing is at stake, call a helpline first and get advice on how to have it.

Q: How do I stop chasing my losses?
A: Make it physically impossible before you negotiate with yourself: a bank block, a self-exclusion, and handing your card to someone. Chasing is one of the strongest markers of a heavy gambling pattern, and it is the phase where the most damage happens fastest.

Q: How many times do people relapse before they stop?
A: There is no reliable number, and any figure quoted as one is invented. What the research does support is that lapses are common in behavioural addiction recovery, and that people who treat them as information rather than verdicts do better than those who treat them as proof of failure.
