# The 9-question gambling self-check (PGSI)
URL: https://trysilex.com/gambling-self-check/
Language: en
Description: Take the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) — the same 9-question screener clinicians and helplines use. Runs entirely in your browser, stores nothing, sends nothing.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: These nine questions are the Problem Gambling Severity Index, the standard screener from the Canadian Problem Gambling Index (Ferris & Wynne, 2001). Score 0–27. A score of 8 or more puts you in the highest-risk band. It runs in your browser — nothing is stored, nothing is sent anywhere, and there is no email box at the end.

The PGSI asks about the last 12 months. Answer for that window, not for your worst month ever and not for last week. Being honest with a page that can't remember your answers is the easiest honesty available.

## How the scoring works
Each of the nine items scores 0 for never, 1 for sometimes, 2 for most of the time and 3 for almost always, giving a total from 0 to 27. The bands come from the Canadian Problem Gambling Index:
Score | Standard band | What it usually means
0 | Non-problem gambling | No indicators reported in the last 12 months.
1–2 | Low risk | Early signs most casual bettors don't report — worth watching.
3–7 | Moderate risk | A heavier pattern, often with some financial or social consequence already.
8–27 | Problem gambling | The highest band on the screener. Most people here benefit from structured help, not willpower alone.

Instrument: Ferris, J. & Wynne, H. (2001), The Canadian Problem Gambling Index: Final Report, Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse. The PGSI is a screening instrument; clinical diagnosis of gambling disorder uses the DSM-5 criteria and requires a qualified clinician.

## Whatever your score, the next step is the same
A number doesn't change anything by itself. Two things do, and both work at any score:
- Put distance between you and the bet. Not willpower — friction. Block gambling on your phone, then add the two layers you can't undo in a craving: self-exclusion and a bank gambling block.
- Learn what the urge actually is. Urges rise, crest and fall, typically within about 20–30 minutes, whether or not you bet. That pattern is the thing to lean on.

## Common questions

Q: What score means I have a gambling problem?
A: On the PGSI, 0 is non-problem gambling, 1–2 is low risk, 3–7 is moderate risk, and 8 or above is the band usually described as problem gambling. But the PGSI is a screener, not a diagnosis — only a qualified clinician can diagnose gambling disorder, using the DSM-5 criteria.

Q: Is this test stored or shared?
A: No. The scoring happens in JavaScript inside your own browser. There is no form submission, no cookie, no analytics event, and no email capture. Closing the tab erases it.

Q: Can I take it about someone else?
A: The PGSI is written in the first person and validated as a self-report, so answering it for a partner or family member gives you a rough impression at best. If you're worried about someone else, the helplines below take calls from family members too.

Q: What if I score low but still feel out of control?
A: Trust that feeling over the number. The PGSI weights financial and social consequences heavily, so someone early in a heavy pattern — or someone gambling money they can technically afford — can score low and still be in trouble.

========================================================================
# Someone you love is gambling
URL: https://trysilex.com/help-someone-with-gambling-addiction/
Language: en
Description: Practical steps for partners and families: protect the household money first, why paying the debt backfires, how to have the conversation, and where to get support for yourself.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Three things, in this order. Protect the essential money first — rent, utilities, food — before anything else, because that is the damage that compounds fastest. Don't clear their debt. Repeatedly covering losses removes the consequence and reliably makes it worse. And get support for yourself, today, without waiting for them to be ready — you don't need their permission, and helplines take calls from family members.

Most guidance written for you is about them — how to spot it, how to persuade them, how to get them into treatment. This page starts somewhere else, because in the first week the thing that actually determines how bad this gets is not whether they're ready to stop. It's whether the household still has rent money in a month.

## First: protect the essential money
Do this before the conversation, before the research, before anything. Not as punishment — as damage control while the rest gets worked out.
- List what must be paid over the next 30 days: housing, utilities, food, transport, childcare, medication, minimum debt payments.
- Move that money somewhere they can't reach — an account in your name only. This is the single highest-value action available to you.
- Check what's joint. Joint accounts, joint credit, overdrafts, savings, and anything with your name on it that they can borrow against. If they can reach it, assume at some point it will be reached.
- Watch for credit taken in your name. Check your own credit file. This is an unpleasant thing to do to someone you love and it is unfortunately common enough to be worth doing.
- Don't lend, don't cover, don't top up. Including small amounts. Including "just this once, so the kids don't notice."

If money is already short, free debt advice is available to you, not only to them — the options are here.

## Why clearing the debt backfires
It is the most natural thing in the world to want to make it go away, and it is the move that most reliably makes the next round bigger. Two reasons:
The consequence is doing work. A debt that gets absorbed by someone else teaches that losses are survivable and someone will catch them, which is precisely the belief that funds the next session. And a cleared balance is, in practice, a fresh line of credit — the most common thing that happens after a bailout is a return to gambling with more room to lose.
This is not a rule about being harsh. Protect the household, protect the children, protect yourself. Just don't route money to the operators through your own account.

## The conversation
You probably won't get one clean, decisive talk, and expecting one sets you up to feel it failed. What tends to work better:
- Pick a calm, sober, private moment. Not right after a discovery, not during a match, not at midnight.
- Describe what you've seen, not what they are. "£800 left the account in three days and I don't know where it went" is hard to argue with. "You're a compulsive gambler" starts a different, unwinnable conversation.
- Expect lying, and don't take it as a verdict on the relationship. Concealment is close to a defining feature of a gambling problem, and shame drives it. Someone lying about this is usually not doing it to you so much as to themselves.
- Say what you're doing regardless of their answer. "I'm moving the bill money" doesn't require agreement.
- Offer a next step, not a diagnosis. A helpline number, one free assessment, or a nine-question self-check they can take privately without telling anyone the result.

Don't issue a threat you're not going to carry out. One boundary you keep is worth more than five you don't.

## If they are ready to act
The things that work are the same regardless of who's asking, and they work better when the person sets them up themselves:
- Self-exclusion — free, and the only layer they can't reverse in a craving.
- A bank gambling block — free, and takes days to lift rather than seconds.
- Blocking on the phone — and if you're holding a Screen Time passcode for them, that's a real, useful role. Just be aware of what it makes you: the person who has to say no at 1am. It works better with a friend than a partner.

## Get support for yourself. Now, not later
You do not have to wait for them to be ready, and you do not need their permission.
- Gam-Anon — peer support specifically for families and partners of gamblers.
- National helplines take your call too. US: 1-800-522-4700, 24/7. UK: GamCare's National Gambling Helpline, 0808 8020 133. You are allowed to ring them about someone else, and they will not tell you to leave.
- Free debt advice — StepChange and National Debtline in the UK, NFCC members in the US.
- Your own therapy, if you can get it. Living with this is its own injury, separate from theirs.

## Two things worth knowing
Gambling harm and suicide risk travel together. If they've said anything that worries you, take it seriously and say so out loud — asking directly does not plant the idea. In the US, 988 answers 24/7; in the UK, Samaritans on 116 123.
None of this is your fault, and you can't do it for them. You can make the environment safer, hold a boundary, and be there when they're ready. What you can't do is want it more than they do — and burning yourself out trying is a real risk, not a hypothetical one.

## Common questions

Q: Should I pay off my partner's gambling debt?
A: Almost always no, however much you want the problem gone. Covering losses softens the consequence the person is meant to be feeling, and the pattern usually repeats at a larger scale. It also puts you in the position of being the thing standing between them and reality, which damages the relationship in a way that is hard to undo. Free debt advisers will help you separate protecting the household from bailing out the gambling.

Q: How do I know if it's really a gambling problem?
A: Secrecy and lying about money are the most common early signals — money missing without explanation, unexplained transfers, defensiveness about phone use, borrowing that doesn't add up. The formal screener is the PGSI, but it's self-report, so it only helps if they take it themselves and answer honestly.

Q: Can I make them stop?
A: No, and the attempt tends to make it more hidden. What you can control is the environment: household money, your own accounts, what you fund. Blocks and self-exclusion are far more effective when the person sets them up themselves, but you can put your own finances out of reach either way.

Q: Should I give them an ultimatum?
A: Threats you won't follow through on cost you credibility and teach them the boundary isn't real. Clear, specific and kept beats dramatic. "I'm moving the bill money into an account in my name" is a boundary. "I'll leave if it happens again" is only a boundary if you'll do it.

Q: Where can family members get help?
A: Gam-Anon runs peer support specifically for families and partners of gamblers. National helplines take calls from affected others as well as gamblers — in the US, 1-800-522-4700; in the UK, GamCare's National Gambling Helpline on 0808 8020 133. None of it requires the gambler's involvement or consent.

========================================================================
# How long do gambling urges last?
URL: https://trysilex.com/how-long-do-gambling-urges-last/
Language: en
Description: A gambling urge behaves like a wave: it rises, crests and falls, usually inside 20 to 30 minutes, whether or not you bet. What the first weeks feel like, and the urge-surfing technique that uses the pattern.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: A single urge usually peaks and passes within about 20 to 30 minutes — and it passes whether or not you gamble. The first one to two weeks after quitting are typically the worst for frequency, with intensity easing over roughly the first 90 days. Betting doesn't end an urge; it teaches your brain that urges get answered, which makes the next one stronger.

The most useful thing anyone told me about cravings is that they are shaped like waves, not like switches. A switch stays on until something turns it off. A wave rises, crests and falls on its own schedule, and there is nothing you have to do to make the fall happen.

## The single urge: roughly 20 to 30 minutes
An individual gambling urge typically peaks and subsides within about twenty to thirty minutes. It is the figure used throughout clinical self-help material on cravings, and the point of it is not precision — it is that the number is small and finite. You are not being asked to resist forever. You are being asked to be somewhere else for half an hour.
Two things distort the estimate while you're in it:
- Clusters. One urge that ends and restarts twice feels like a ninety-minute urge. It isn't; it's three waves and two gaps you didn't notice.
- Cue exposure. If the trigger stays in front of you — the app icon, the match on TV, the promo email — the wave keeps getting re-launched. This is why removing cues matters more than resisting them: block the access and get off the marketing lists.

## The first weeks: worse before better
Frequency is usually highest in the first one to two weeks, then declines unevenly. Intensity tends to ease across roughly the first three months — which is why 90 days is a common frame for structured programs, including the one in Silex.
Expect the curve to be lumpy rather than smooth. Predictable spikes cluster around:
- Money arriving — payday, a bonus, a tax refund.
- Fixtures and events — the start of a season, a final, a big race. (If sport is your trigger, that's a specific problem with a specific fix.)
- The old time slot — if you gambled at 11pm, 11pm will ask about it.
- Emotional states you used to gamble at — boredom, loneliness, stress, and, for a lot of people, feeling good and wanting to celebrate.

Anna Lembke's framing in Dopamine Nation is the clearest short explanation of why the early part feels bad: the pleasure and pain systems share a balance, and after heavy stimulation the balance sits tilted towards discomfort for a while before it resets. Knowing that the low mood in week one is a recovery signal rather than evidence you have ruined yourself makes it much easier to sit through.

## Why betting doesn't end the urge
It feels like it does, and that is the trap. The relief that arrives when you place a bet is mostly the removal of the discomfort the craving created — not a gain, just a return to baseline. Then the reward system draws its conclusion: urges get answered. Next time it asks louder and sooner.
The reverse is also true and much less discussed: every urge you ride out is evidence in the other direction. It is not willpower being spent; it's a pattern being unlearned. That is why the tenth wave is genuinely easier than the first — not because you got tougher, but because the prediction changed.

## Urge surfing: what to actually do for 30 minutes
Urge surfing comes from relapse-prevention work (G. Alan Marlatt and colleagues) and it deliberately avoids both fighting the craving and obeying it:
- Name it. "This is an urge. It's about a 7." Rating it converts a flood into an observation, which is a smaller thing.
- Slow your breathing. Four in, four hold, four out, four hold, for a few minutes. It won't remove the craving; it takes the alarm response down enough to think.
- Find it in your body. Chest, stomach, hands, jaw. Notice whether it is rising or falling right now. Cravings feel infinite in the abstract and specific when inspected.
- Set a timer and stay busy. Twenty minutes, doing something that occupies hands and eyes — a walk, a shower, washing up, anything physical. Not sitting still with your phone in your hand.
- Re-read why you stopped. Your own words from a calm day beat any argument you can construct at peak craving.
- Tell someone, if there is someone. "I'm having a bad one" is a complete sentence, and saying it out loud reliably takes the top off it.

Silex builds this into one button that is never behind the paywall — rate the urge, breathe, then a timer with your own reasons and your money-kept total on screen while the wave passes. The sequence matters more than the app: it works from a kitchen timer and a note in your wallet.

## What the pattern means for how you plan
If urges are short and self-limiting, then the whole game is surviving thirty minutes without access. That reframes what a blocker is for. It doesn't have to be permanent or unbreakable — it has to outlast half an hour:
- A DNS-level block buys minutes.
- A bank block with a 48-hour cooling-off buys two days.
- Self-exclusion buys months or years.

Stack them and the wave has nowhere to land. And if one does land — what you do in the hour afterwards matters far more than the slip itself.
For how the frequency changes over the first three months, and which weeks people actually relapse in, see the week-by-week timeline.

## Common questions

Q: How long does a gambling craving last?
A: Most pass within 20 to 30 minutes. Some are shorter, a few come in clusters that feel continuous for an hour or two, especially in the first week or around a trigger like payday or a big match. What matters more than the exact number is that they end on their own.

Q: Do gambling urges ever go away completely?
A: They become far less frequent and much easier to ignore, but many people get an occasional flicker years later — usually attached to a specific cue like walking past a shop or a sporting event. That is normal and is not a sign the recovery failed. It just means the cue is still a cue.

Q: Why do urges get worse right after I quit?
A: Because you have removed the thing that used to answer them, and the reward system briefly escalates its demand. It is the same shape as any withdrawal curve — the worst part is at the front, which is unfortunately when your evidence that it works is thinnest.

Q: What is urge surfing?
A: A technique from relapse-prevention work: instead of fighting the craving or obeying it, you observe it — where it sits in your body, whether it is rising or falling — and let it crest and drop. You are riding it out rather than white-knuckling it, which is why it doesn't exhaust you the way suppression does.

Q: Does an urge mean I'm about to relapse?
A: No. Urges are extremely common in early recovery and most of them lead nowhere. Treating a craving as a prediction of failure tends to make the failure likelier — a slip is far more often preceded by the thought 'I've already blown it' than by a strong urge.

========================================================================
# How to stop gambling
URL: https://trysilex.com/how-to-stop-gambling/
Language: en
Description: A practical, evidence-based plan for quitting gambling: the three barriers to put up first, how to ride out an urge, what the first 90 days look like, and where to get free human help.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Quitting gambling is three separate jobs, done in this order. One: put up barriers that don't depend on how you feel — self-exclusion, a bank block, a device block. Two: learn to sit through a 20–30 minute urge without acting on it. Three: replace what gambling was doing for you, which takes months, not days. Willpower is what you use in the gaps between those three, not instead of them.

Almost every guide to quitting gambling is a list of tips that assume the reader will be rational at the moment of decision. The whole problem is that you won't be. So this plan is built the other way round: make the decisions now, while you're calm, that remove the need to decide later.

## Step 1 — Barriers that don't depend on how you feel
Do these three today. Together they take about half an hour and cost nothing, and they are ranked by how hard they are to undo, strongest first.
- Self-exclude. In the UK, one free GAMSTOP registration covers every UK-licensed online operator for 6 months, 1 year or 5 years. In the US, register with your state programme and with each sportsbook individually. This is the only layer you genuinely cannot reverse in a craving.
- Get your bank to decline gambling payments. Most UK banks offer this in-app with a 48–72 hour cooling-off before it lifts; Monzo lets you set up to 12 months. In the US, ask your issuer to block merchant category code 7995.
- Block it on your phone. A device-wide DNS profile covers every app and browser on Wi-Fi and cellular, and stops reinstalls if someone else holds the passcode — on iPhone or on Android. Which blocker to use →

Then close the two routes people forget: unsubscribe from every gambling email and turn off every push notification, and unlink e-wallets and prepaid cards from operator accounts. Sportsbook marketing is timed and targeted; it is not neutral information arriving at a random moment.

## Step 2 — Learn what an urge actually does
A gambling urge typically peaks and passes within 20 to 30 minutes, and it passes whether or not you bet. Betting doesn't end an urge — it teaches your brain that urges get answered, which makes the next one arrive sooner and louder.
So the skill is narrow and learnable: be somewhere else for half an hour. Rate the urge out of ten, slow your breathing, notice where it sits in your body, set a timer, do something physical, re-read your own reasons for stopping, and tell someone if there is someone to tell.
The full urge-surfing method, and what the first weeks feel like →

## Step 3 — Replace what gambling was doing for you
This is the step that gets skipped, and the reason people relapse at week six with all their blocks still switched on. Gambling was doing a job. Until something else does that job, the vacancy stays open.
Work out which one it was, because the replacement differs:
What gambling gave you | What tends to actually fill it
Escape — switching your head off | Anything genuinely absorbing and low-stakes: exercise, games, a craft, long walks. The requirement is absorption, not virtue.
The rush — action, stakes, adrenaline | Real stakes with real recovery: sport, competition, climbing, performing, anything with a scoreboard that isn't money.
Chasing — winning back what you lost | A concrete debt plan, so the hole has a route out that isn't a bet. Free advice from StepChange, National Debtline or an NFCC member.
Company — the app was always there | People, on a schedule you don't have to feel motivated to keep: a group, a regular game, a standing call.

This is why 90 days is the usual frame for structured programs: it's roughly how long it takes for the urges to thin out and for something else to be in place.

## Get a human involved
Not a substitute for the above — a multiplier on it. All of these are free:
- A national helpline. They take calls from people who are nowhere near ready to quit, and from family members. Numbers are at the bottom of this page.
- Gamblers Anonymous or SMART Recovery. Two very different traditions — one fellowship-based, one cognitive-behavioural and secular. Try both before deciding groups aren't for you.
- Treatment. CBT for gambling disorder has the strongest evidence base of any psychological treatment here. In the UK it is available on the NHS through the National Gambling Support Network; in the US, coverage varies by state and by insurer, and your state council on problem gambling can point you at what's local.
- Free debt advice, if money is the immediate pressure. Debt and chasing feed each other, and dealing with one makes the other much easier.

## What doesn't work
- Deciding to be more disciplined. Not because you're weak — because gambling products are engineered to defeat exactly that. Variable rewards, near-misses and losses dressed as wins are design decisions, documented in detail in Natasha Dow Schüll's Addiction by Design.
- Keeping one account "just for the big games". This is the single most common way a serious attempt ends.
- A blocker as your only move. One minute to remove, and no plan behind it.
- Secrecy. Hiding it is the mechanism that lets it grow. Telling one person is the highest-leverage unpleasant thing on this page.
- Waiting for rock bottom. There isn't a floor that arrives and fixes this. People stop from wherever they happen to be standing.

## Related, depending on where you are
- Betting on sport specifically? The cue problem is different — how to stop sports betting.
- Want to know what the next three months feel like? The week-by-week timeline, including the weeks people actually relapse in.
- Debt behind you? Where to start with gambling debt.
- Reading this about someone else? What actually helps — and what makes it worse.

## Where to start, if you only do one thing
Take the 9-question PGSI self-check — two minutes, nothing stored — and then do whichever barrier in Step 1 you're most reluctant about. The reluctance is usually pointing at the one that would work.
And if you've already slipped: the next hour matters more than the slip does.

## Common questions

Q: Can I stop gambling on my own?
A: Some people do, and the ones who succeed almost always change their environment rather than relying on resolve — blocks, self-exclusion, no access to money, someone who knows. If you have tried alone more than twice, that is information about the method, not about you: adding a helpline, a group, or a therapist raises the odds substantially and costs nothing in most countries.

Q: Is it better to cut down or stop completely?
A: For anyone in the moderate or high-risk bands on the PGSI, complete abstinence is usually the more achievable target, because controlled gambling requires you to make a good decision every single time in the exact state where decisions are worst. Cutting down can work for lower-risk patterns. Be honest about which one you are.

Q: How long does it take to stop gambling?
A: The urges thin out fastest in the first two weeks and keep easing across roughly three months. Rebuilding the parts of life gambling took over — money, sleep, relationships, how you spend a Saturday — takes longer, and is the part that decides whether it lasts.

Q: What is the first thing I should do today?
A: Self-exclude from every operator you have an account with, and ask your bank for a gambling block. Both are free, both take under twenty minutes, and unlike anything you install, neither can be undone in the ninety seconds when it matters.

Q: Does gambling addiction ever fully go away?
A: Most people reach a point where it stops running their life and stops occupying their thinking. Occasional cue-triggered flickers years later are common and are not a sign of failure. The practical goal is a life where gambling is irrelevant, not a brain that has never heard of it.

========================================================================
# How to stop sports betting
URL: https://trysilex.com/how-to-stop-sports-betting/
Language: en
Description: Sports betting is harder to quit than casino gambling because the trigger is the sport itself. What to block, what to do about watching games, and how to handle the group chat.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Sports betting has a problem other gambling doesn't: the trigger is a thing you love and don't want to give up. So blocking the apps isn't enough — you also have to break the link between watching and betting. Close every account properly (self-exclusion, not deletion), block at the DNS and bank level, kill the odds notifications, and expect the first month of fixtures to be the hardest part.

Quitting a casino app means avoiding a place. Quitting sports betting means staying in a place you like — the sport, the group chat, the Saturday — while removing one thing from it. That's a harder problem, and most generic quit-gambling advice ignores it entirely.

## Why this one's different
- The cue is everywhere and you don't want it gone. Odds are read out during coverage, printed on the screen, embedded in the highlights app and pushed to your phone. Nobody expects you to stop caring about football.
- It feels like skill. That's the trap unique to sports. When a slots player loses, they know it was chance. When a bettor loses, they conclude they misread the injury news — so the answer feels like more research, which means more bets.
- It's social. The group chat with everyone's slips in it is a genuine friendship, and quitting can feel like leaving it.
- Live betting removed the gaps. In-play markets turned a single pre-match bet into a decision every few minutes for ninety minutes.

## Step 1: close the accounts properly
Deleting apps does almost nothing — the mobile site works, reinstalling takes seconds, and your balance and card are still sitting there. Self-exclude instead. It closes the account, stops them serving you, and can't be undone in a bad moment.
- UK: one free GAMSTOP registration covers every UK-licensed online operator, for 6 months, 1 year or 5 years. Betting shops are a separate scheme — do that too if you use them.
- US: each sportsbook has self-exclusion in its responsible-gaming settings, and most states run their own programme. Do every operator you hold an account with, dormant ones included.

Full self-exclusion guide, including what it misses →

## Step 2: block the routes back
- Device-wide DNS blocking. Covers every app and browser, on Wi-Fi and cellular — not just Safari. Setup on iPhone → on Android →
- A bank gambling block. Most UK banks offer one in-app with a 48–72 hour cooling-off; in the US, ask your issuer about merchant code 7995. How →
- Kill the notifications. This is the sports-specific one everyone skips. Turn off push from every sportsbook and from score apps that carry odds. Unsubscribe from betting emails. Mute the odds segments where you can.

## Step 3: break the watching–betting link
This is the part that decides whether it holds past the first month.
Betting and watching became one activity. Until they're separate again, every kickoff is a craving cue. Practical version:
- Take a few weeks off live games. Not forever — long enough that "match on" stops meaning "slip on". Highlights are much weaker cues than live.
- Change what you do with your hands. Watch with someone, at a friend's, at a pub, anywhere your phone isn't the second screen. The living-room-alone-with-phone setup is the highest-risk configuration there is.
- Give the stake a job. Some people move their usual stake into a savings pot at kickoff. It sounds gimmicky and it works, because the ritual survives while the outcome stops being financial.
- Plan the group chat. You don't owe anyone an explanation, but decide what you'll say before it comes up. "I've stopped betting, still here for the football" ends the conversation faster than dodging it for a month.

## Step 4: the first month of fixtures
Expect predictable spikes rather than a smooth decline — the start of a season, a derby, a final, a big race meeting, and the moment your accumulator would have come in. Urges peak and pass in roughly 20 to 30 minutes whether or not you bet. The urge-surfing method is here →
One specific trap for bettors: the near-miss you'd have won. You will, early on, watch a result land that would have paid. That's not evidence you should have bet — it's the same variable reward that kept you in, arriving without costing you anything this time. Notice it, name it, let it pass.

## What to do about the money already lost
Sports bettors tend to be chasing more than casino players, because "I know this sport" makes recovery feel achievable. It isn't, and chasing is where most of the real damage happens. If there's debt behind you, deal with it as its own problem rather than as something to win back — free options are here, and none of them involve a bet.
Work out what it's actually cost so far →

## If you slip
Very common in the first season, and not the end of it. The hour afterwards matters far more than the bet does — here's what to do in it.

## Common questions

Q: Why is sports betting so hard to quit?
A: Because the cue never goes away. Someone quitting slots can avoid casinos; you can't avoid sport without giving up something you actually enjoy, and every match, highlight reel and group chat carries a betting prompt with it. On top of that, sports betting feels like skill rather than chance, so losses read as bad research instead of an expected outcome — which makes chasing feel rational.

Q: Can I keep watching sport if I quit betting?
A: Most people can, eventually, but not usually in month one. The honest sequence is: stop betting first, take a break from live-watching for a few weeks while the association weakens, then come back to the sport deliberately. If you go straight back to watching with the app still on your phone, you're testing willpower during the exact ninety seconds it's weakest.

Q: Should I delete the app or self-exclude?
A: Self-exclude. Deleting the app takes fifteen seconds to undo and leaves your account funded and waiting. Self-exclusion closes the account and stops them serving you, and you cannot reverse it in a craving. Do it with every sportsbook you hold an account with, including the dormant ones.

Q: What about free bets and promos they send when I stop?
A: Expect them, and expect them to be well timed — operators run reactivation campaigns at people who have gone quiet. Self-exclusion should remove you from marketing; if the messages keep coming, that is a compliance failure worth reporting to the regulator. Unsubscribe, block the sender, and turn off every push notification from sports apps too.

Q: Is fantasy sports or prediction-market trading a safe substitute?
A: For most people in recovery, no. Daily fantasy with entry fees, and prediction markets with sports contracts, deliver the same loop — stake, uncertainty, outcome tied to a match — with a different label on the button. If the appeal is having something riding on the game, that's the pattern to break, not to re-house.

# How the program was built, and from what
URL: https://trysilex.com/methodology/
Language: en
Description: The clinical and academic sources behind Silex's 90-day quit-gambling program: CBT for gambling disorder, the PGSI self-check, relapse-prevention research, and the literature on how gambling products are engineered.

Silex's 90 days were written from published clinical material and research, not from a marketing brief. This page lists what they were built from so you can check the work — and so you can go to the primary sources directly if you'd rather not pay for an app.

## The shape of the program
90 authored days, one lesson at a time, in three phases:
Phase | Idea | What it draws on
See the Machine | It was engineered. Drop the shame. | Research on how gambling products are designed — variable-ratio reinforcement, losses disguised as wins, near-miss effects, machine-zone immersion
Rewire | Your brain is resetting. Trust the timeline. | CBT for gambling disorder: trigger mapping, cognitive restructuring of gambling beliefs, urge exposure and urge surfing, behavioural substitution
Fortify | Build the life that competes. | Relapse-prevention planning, values work, financial repair, rebuilding the activities gambling crowded out

A lapse doesn't reset anything. It routes you to a Reset day built around relapse-prevention material on the abstinence violation effect — the finding that how a person interprets a slip predicts whether it becomes a full return to gambling more reliably than the slip itself does.

## The sources

### Clinical treatment material
- Nancy M. Petry's cognitive-behavioural work on pathological gambling — the standard CBT framework for gambling disorder: functional analysis of gambling episodes, trigger identification, coping-skills training and planned alternative activities. Petry's treatment manual and trials are the backbone of Phase 2.
- The UCLA Gambling Studies Program patient workbook — a free, publicly available self-help workbook. Several of the day-level exercise formats (trigger inventories, urge logs, decision worksheets) follow its structure.
- Motivational Interviewing (William R. Miller & Stephen Rollnick) — why the program asks rather than lectures, and why your own stated reasons for quitting are resurfaced back to you instead of the app supplying motivation.
- Relapse Prevention (G. Alan Marlatt & Judith R. Gordon, 1985) — high-risk-situation planning, the abstinence violation effect, and the design rule that a slip must never zero your history.
- SMART Recovery and Gamblers Anonymous — two different traditions, both pointed to inside the app, because the evidence does not support telling someone there is only one route.

### How gambling products are engineered
- Natasha Dow Schüll, Addiction by Design: Machine Gambling in Las Vegas (Princeton University Press, 2012) — the ethnography behind Phase 1. The "machine zone", the design of continuous play, and the industry's own language about time-on-device.
- Anna Lembke, Dopamine Nation (2021) — the pleasure–pain balance framing used to explain why the first weeks feel worse before they feel better.
- Allen Carr's method — the argument that the "relief" a bet provides is the withdrawal it created, adapted to gambling rather than smoking.

### Measurement
- The Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI), from the Canadian Problem Gambling Index (Ferris & Wynne, 2001) — nine items over a 12-month window, the instrument behind both the app's intake and the self-check on this site. It is a screening tool: it estimates risk, it does not diagnose anyone.

## What we're careful about
- The program is not a clinical trial. Silex applies material from evidence-based treatment; that is not the same as Silex itself having been trialled. Nobody has run a randomised study on this app, and until somebody has, we won't imply otherwise or quote an effectiveness figure.
- Screening is not diagnosis. Every risk score in the app and on this site carries the same line: this isn't a diagnosis, it's a snapshot of risk based on a standard self-check.
- Helplines are re-verified every release, because the numbers do change — the US national line changed in January 2026.
- The program is in English only for now, and its self-exclusion and debt guidance is deepest for the United States and the United Kingdom.

If you spot something in the program that misrepresents a source, write to support@trysilex.com — that is a bug and it gets fixed like one.

# Privacy Policy
URL: https://trysilex.com/privacy/
Language: en
Description: Silex stores nothing about you on any server, holds no accounts, and cannot read anything you write in the app. The full GDPR and UK GDPR notice, including the few places data does leave your phone.

Last updated: 29 October 2026. Canonical version of this notice; it replaces the Notion-hosted copy linked from older builds of the app.
Silex is built on one principle: your recovery is nobody's dataset.
We store nothing about you on any server, hold no accounts, and have no way to read anything you write in this app. (The one piece of code we run on a server is the optional Notion connector in §14, which keeps nothing.) One third party does run a server that receives something: an analytics service is sent the names of the screens you reach, and there is a switch in Settings that stops it. This page explains exactly what that means — including the few places where data does leave your phone, because a privacy policy that only lists the reassuring parts is not a privacy policy.
This notice is written to meet the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the UK GDPR. If you are in the EEA or the UK, the sections on legal bases, transfers and your rights apply to you in full.

## 1. What you enter stays on your device
Everything you record — quiz answers, check-ins, journal reflections, program answers, urge logs, lapse entries, streak dates, money figures, your signature and your orb collection — is stored in two places, both of which belong to you:
- On your iPhone, in the app's local database.
- In your private iCloud, via Apple CloudKit's private database, so your history survives a lost or replaced device.

Your private iCloud database is accessible only to your Apple ID. We are not a party to it and cannot read it. If iCloud is unavailable or disabled, the app stores data only on your device.
We never receive this content. There is no API call that sends it, no backup on our side, and no key that would let us decrypt it. Because we have no access to it and no ability to use it, we do not consider ourselves the controller of what you write in the app — you are. We describe it here for transparency, not because we process it.

## 2. What actually reaches anyone else
Five narrow cases, all optional or technically unavoidable.

### Purchases — Apple, and RevenueCat
Subscriptions are processed by Apple. We use RevenueCat to verify and manage subscription status. It acts as our processor and receives:
- device type and operating system,
- last-seen time, and Apple receipt files,
- optionally, a user identifier and attribution metadata.

It never receives your journal, answers, streak or any recovery content. See Apple's privacy policy and RevenueCat's privacy policy.

### The DNS shield — only if you turn it on
This installs an encrypted-DNS (DoH) configuration so gambling domains fail to resolve across your apps and browsers. While it is on, your device's DNS lookups are answered by Mullvad's public resolver under their no-logging policy. Advanced users may point it at their own NextDNS configuration instead. Mullvad or NextDNS act as independent controllers for those lookups under their own policies — we are not in that path and never see your browsing. Turning the shield off in iOS Settings ends this immediately.

### Blocklist updates
The app periodically downloads public gambling-domain lists from jsDelivr and GitHub. As with any file download, those servers can see the request and your IP address. The request carries no identifier and nothing about you or your recovery.

### Usage counts — the tally on your device
The app keeps a first-party tally of how the app is used (for example, how many times a screen was opened on a given day), stored as counts by day in a single file in the app's own storage. It contains no identifiers and no content you wrote, and that file never leaves your phone. Deleting the app deletes it. The same event names are separately sent to TelemetryDeck unless you turn that off — which is the next section, and the honest reason this one no longer says "reach no one".

### Usage analytics — TelemetryDeck, unless you switch it off
To see where people abandon onboarding — the difference between fixing a screen and guessing at it — the app sends the names of the steps it reaches to TelemetryDeck GmbH, Von-der-Tann-Str. 54, 86159 Augsburg, Germany. What is sent:
- the name of each onboarding step reached and its position in the sequence (funnel.question_04, funnel.paywall), each one at most once per install;
- the names of other in-app events — a program day completed, the panic button opened — and nothing about them beyond the name;
- TelemetryDeck's own default payload: operating-system version, device model, locale, region, app version and similar;
- a random identifier minted by the app for this install.

What is never sent: your quiz answers, your PGSI score, your weekly spend, your journal text, your lapse records — anything you wrote or chose. The signal is that a screen was reached, never what was on it and never what you put into it.
About that identifier. It is a random UUID the app generates on first run. It is deliberately not identifierForVendor, the identifier iOS would otherwise have used, because that one survives deleting and reinstalling the app and is shared with every other app from the same developer. Ours is shared with nothing and dies when you delete the app. Before it leaves your phone it is hashed with a salt on the device; when it arrives, TelemetryDeck adds its own salt and hashes it again, so neither we nor they can work back from the stored value to the original. A single hash would only be pseudonymisation, which is why they do the second one.
We also switch off two things TelemetryDeck would otherwise collect: the session-began signal, and session statistics.
The switch. Settings → Your data → Share anonymous usage. It is on by default, and the reason is not a good look dressed up: an opt-in funnel measures the wrong population, because the people who quit on the first screen are exactly the people who never reach a consent prompt, so the drop-off being measured would be the thing biasing the sample. The price of that default is saying plainly what is sent, which is what this section is for. Turning it off stops new signals immediately, removes the sink from the app, and deletes the batch of unsent signals waiting on disk. What has already gone cannot be recalled — and nothing in it points back to you.
In the App Store's own vocabulary, the app declares no tracking (NSPrivacyTracking false, no tracking domains) and two collected data types — Product Interaction and Device ID — both marked not linked to your identity and not used for tracking, for the single purpose of analytics. See TelemetryDeck's privacy policy.
Nothing else. Those four network paths are the only ones the app has. There are no advertising identifiers, no cross-app tracking, and no profiling or automated decision-making that produces legal or similarly significant effects.

## 3. Legal bases (GDPR Art. 6 and Art. 9)
What | Purpose | Legal basis
Purchase & subscription status (via Apple / RevenueCat) | Provide and restore the subscription you bought; prevent fraudulent entitlement | Art. 6(1)(b) — performance of a contract with you
IP address visible to the blocklist CDN when the app downloads a list | Deliver the blocking feature the app exists to provide | Art. 6(1)(f) — legitimate interests (keeping protection lists current). Our assessment: minimal data, no profiling, no linkage to you
Event names, a hashed install-scoped identifier and TelemetryDeck's default device payload, while "Share anonymous usage" is on | See where people abandon onboarding, so the screens that lose them can be fixed | Art. 6(1)(f) — legitimate interests (making the app work for the people it is meant for). Our assessment: no content, no advertising identifier, an identifier that cannot follow you between apps or survive deleting the app, and a switch in Settings that ends it. The switch is what carries the balancing test — an interest you can refuse in one tap is not one being asserted over you
DNS lookups, while the shield is enabled | Block gambling domains device-wide | Art. 6(1)(a) — your consent, given by enabling the shield and approving the iOS dialog; withdrawable at any time by turning it off
What you write in the app | Deliver the recovery programme to you on your own device | We do not receive it, so we carry out no processing to justify. To the extent it is processed at all, it is on your device under your control

Special-category (health) data. What you record here reveals information about health and about a possible behavioural addiction, which is special-category data under Art. 9. That is exactly why the app is designed the way it is: that data never reaches us, so we never rely on an Art. 9 condition for it.
The harder question is the analytics, and we would rather work through it than wave it away. A signal reading funnel.question_04 carries no content — but Silex is a gambling-recovery app, and the Court of Justice has held that data which only indirectly reveals a special category is caught all the same (Case C-184/20, OT). So we do not claim these signals are innocuous by subject matter: "this install walked into Silex's onboarding" says something adjacent to health about whoever was holding the phone. What we rely on is the other half of Art. 9, which bites on data concerning an identified or identifiable natural person. The identifier attached to these signals is random, minted for a single install, salted and hashed on your device, then salted again with TelemetryDeck's own salt and rehashed on arrival — so no party to it, us included, can work back to a person or match it against anything else. On that basis we treat what reaches TelemetryDeck as outside Art. 9, while still treating it as pseudonymous personal data under Art. 6 and giving it a lawful basis and a working opt-out, because the more cautious of the two readings is the one worth being wrong in. A subscription receipt is unchanged: it does not reveal a health condition beyond the fact that you bought an app.
This is the one paragraph here where competent lawyers can reasonably land in different places, and we would rather say so than let it read as settled.

## 4. International transfers
RevenueCat is a US company (Brandon, Florida) storing data on Amazon Web Services in the United States. Transfers are covered by its data processing agreement, which incorporates the European Commission's Standard Contractual Clauses (Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914), Module Two — controller to processor. For the UK it additionally applies the ICO's International Data Transfer Addendum of 21 March 2022, and for Switzerland the SCCs adapted to the Swiss FADP. RevenueCat is not certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework; the SCCs are the mechanism. Verified against RevenueCat's published DPA on 6 August 2026.
TelemetryDeck is a German company (TelemetryDeck GmbH, Augsburg). It states that usage data is stored exclusively within the European Union, on Hetzner infrastructure in Nuremberg, with parts of the pipeline still running on Azure in Amsterdam and AWS in Frankfurt and a stated plan to consolidate onto Hetzner during 2026. Its corporate privacy policy names those counterparties as Hetzner Online GmbH (Germany), Microsoft Ireland Operations Ltd (Ireland) and Amazon Web Services, Inc. (Seattle, United States) — the AWS entity is American, but the region it stores in is Frankfurt. On TelemetryDeck's own account, then, no analytics data of ours leaves the EEA and no Chapter V transfer mechanism is engaged, because there is no third-country transfer to cover. We have not independently verified those storage regions and cannot; we are reporting what TelemetryDeck publishes.
One thing we cannot give you, and it is why this entry is longer than RevenueCat's. TelemetryDeck offers no Art. 28 processor agreement. Its data processing terms are automatically part of its Terms of Service, so there is nothing to sign — but they state that it acts "neither as a processor within the meaning of Article 4(8) of the GDPR nor as a joint controller", and that Articles 26 and 28 do not apply, on the ground that what it receives is anonymous rather than personal data. We have not adopted that position: we treat the hashed install identifier as pseudonymous personal data, give it an Art. 6 basis and an opt-out regardless (§3), and describe TelemetryDeck as a processor in substance because that is what it is doing. The consequence you should know about is that the guarantees an Art. 28 contract would carry — documented instructions, audit rights, a contractual deletion obligation — are not available to us from this vendor, because it declines the role that creates them. Verified against TelemetryDeck's published privacy policy, data processing agreement and architecture & security pages on 17 August 2026.
Apple — see Apple's privacy policy for its own transfer safeguards. Your private iCloud data is governed by Apple's terms and is not transferred by us, because we never hold it.
Us. We are established in Ukraine, which is outside the EEA and has no European Commission adequacy decision. Where you give data to us directly, that is a direct collection rather than a Chapter V transfer (per EDPB Guidelines 05/2021 on the interplay of Art. 3 and Chapter V). In practice there is almost nothing to collect: there is no account, and the only personal data we can see is the pseudonymous subscription record in RevenueCat's dashboard and the aggregate counts in TelemetryDeck's.

## 5. How long anything is kept
- On your device and in your private iCloud: until you delete it. We cannot delete it for you, and we cannot stop you deleting it.
- On our systems: nothing, because we operate none. The only third-party server holding anything of ours is TelemetryDeck's — see below.
- Purchase records: retained by Apple and RevenueCat under their own retention schedules, and as required by tax and accounting law.
- Usage counts on your device: removed when the app is deleted.
- Event names held by TelemetryDeck: it publishes no deletion schedule for them. Its plans quote a retention figure — 90 days on the free tier, longer on paid ones — but that is a query window: how far back its dashboards can look. Data older than the window is moved to cold storage rather than deleted, and can be loaded back. TelemetryDeck says deletion, one-off or on a schedule, can be arranged on request; we have not arranged one, so assume these signals persist indefinitely. Since they are counts carrying no identifier that reaches back to you, that is a smaller statement than it sounds — but it is the accurate one, and we would rather print it than a number we made up.

## 6. Who is responsible
Controller: Kyrylo Lozovyi
Address: Vidpochinku 12, Kyiv, Ukraine
Privacy contact: support@trysilex.com (also reachable at stopgamblesupport@gmail.com, the address shown inside current builds of the app)
We have not appointed a Data Protection Officer; we are not required to, because we carry out no large-scale monitoring and hold no special-category data on our systems (see §3).

## 7. Your rights
If you are in the EEA or UK you have the right to access your data, to rectification, to erasure, to restriction of processing, to data portability, to object to processing based on legitimate interests, and to withdraw consent at any time where consent is the basis (the DNS shield — withdraw by turning it off; this does not affect processing already carried out).
An honest limitation. For almost everything this app touches, we hold no identifiable data about you and no account that could link a request to a person. Under GDPR Art. 11 we are not required to obtain extra information purely to identify you, and we will not ask you for identity documents to service a request we have no data to answer. In practice:
- Content you wrote — exercise these rights directly: it is on your device and in your iCloud, and deleting the app (plus the iCloud copy) erases it completely.
- Purchase data — contact Apple, or contact us and we will pass the request to RevenueCat, which acts as our processor.
- Usage analytics — your Art. 21 right to object to our legitimate interests has a switch rather than a support queue: Settings → Your data → Share anonymous usage, off. It stops new signals immediately, removes the sink and deletes the batch waiting on disk. You do not have to write to us and you do not have to give a reason. What was already sent cannot be pulled back, and cannot be found again either, because nothing in it identifies you.

Write to support@trysilex.com and we will respond within one month, as required by Art. 12(3).
Right to complain. You may lodge a complaint with your national data protection authority. The list is at edpb.europa.eu; in the UK it is the ICO. You do not have to contact us first, though we would rather you did.

## 8. Deleting everything
- Delete the app from your iPhone.
- Remove the iCloud copy: Settings → your name → iCloud → Manage Account Storage → Silex.
- Cancel a subscription: Settings → your name → Subscriptions, or the Manage Subscription link in the app.

## 9. Sensitive information, and why the design is the policy
What you record here concerns your health and your finances, and we treat it that way. No accounts to breach, no servers of ours to subpoena, and nothing held by any vendor that could be read back as your recovery. The strongest protection we can offer is not holding your data at all — and that part is structural rather than a promise: there is no key, no backup and no copy, so there is nothing to quietly reverse a decision about.
What changed. Until August 2026 this section also said there was no analytics vendor holding a copy. That is no longer true: TelemetryDeck holds a count of how many installs reached each screen. It is a real reduction in the guarantee and we are not going to call it anything else. What survives is the part doing the work — the content stays on your phone, the identifier attached to those counts cannot be tied to you or followed between apps, and the whole thing has a switch. What we gave up is the ability to say the word none.

## 10. Children
Silex is intended for adults and is not directed at children. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 18. The App Store listing is rated accordingly.

## 11. Changes
If this policy changes, the date at the top changes and the current version is always published at this address.
Adding TelemetryDeck is a material change, and the previous version of this section promised that material changes would be surfaced in the app. We have amended that promise rather than claim we kept it. The app has no mechanism that shows a notice on update, and we are not going to describe one that does not exist. What this release actually does is put the switch in Settings with a plain description of what is sent beside it — visible to anyone who looks, not pushed at anyone who does not. That is less than the old sentence promised, which is exactly why the sentence had to change rather than the account of what happened.
So the promise now reads: material changes are named in this section and in the App Store release notes of the version that makes them, and any change that widens what leaves your device ships with the control for it in the same release.

## 12. Contact
support@trysilex.com

## 13. The free browser extension
This notice also covers Silex — Free Gambling Blocker, the browser extension for Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Firefox. It is simpler than the app, and so is this section:
- It collects nothing. No account, no analytics, no identifiers, and it makes no network requests of its own. Nothing about you or your browsing is sent to us or to anyone else.
- How it blocks. The extension carries a list of gambling domains inside it. Your browser compares the pages you open against that list locally, using its built-in declarativeNetRequest feature. The browser does not report back to the extension, or to us, which sites you visit or which were blocked.
- Why it asks for access to all sites. Browsers only let an extension replace a blocked page with its own help page — instead of showing an error — if it holds access to the sites involved. That access is used for nothing else: the extension does not read, change or collect the content of any page.
- The help page shows crisis lines and links to this website. Following a link is an ordinary visit to trysilex.com, covered by the rest of this notice.
- Reporting a missed site opens your own email app. What you send is up to you; we use it only to update the list and reply.
- Removing the extension removes it and everything in it.

The domain list is derived from The Blocklist Project (public domain) and the UT1 lists of Université Toulouse Capitole (CC BY-SA 4.0).

## 14. The Notion recovery tracker
Silex Recovery Tracker for Notion is an optional, free connector that sets up a recovery tracker page in your own Notion workspace. It has nothing to do with the app: using one does not touch the other.
- What runs, and where. A small function we wrote, hosted by Cloudflare. It runs only for the few seconds after you click Connect and approve access in Notion.
- What it receives. Notion sends it a one-time code, which it swaps for an access token to your workspace. Notion's reply also includes your workspace name and your Notion profile (name, and possibly email and avatar). The function reads only the token and ignores the rest.
- What it does with the token. It creates one page, two tables and two example rows in your workspace, then sends you to that page. It does not read or search your existing pages, except — only if Notion refuses a top-level page — to find the one page you chose to share, so the tracker can go inside it.
- What it keeps. Nothing. The token exists only in memory for that one request; there is no database, no file and no copy of anything you write in the tracker. We cannot open your tracker afterwards, and if Notion returns an error, only Notion's error code is logged, never workspace content.
- Removing it. In Notion, go to Settings → Connections and remove Silex. The tracker stays: it's an ordinary page that belongs to you. Delete it like any other page.

Legal basis: the request you make by clicking Connect (GDPR Art. 6(1)(b)). Cloudflare processes the connection itself (your IP address and request headers) as our processor; see Cloudflare's privacy policy. What you write in the tracker is between you and Notion, under Notion's privacy policy.

========================================================================
# Self-exclusion: the strongest block there is
URL: https://trysilex.com/self-exclusion-guide/
Language: en
Description: How gambling self-exclusion works in the UK via GAMSTOP and in the US state by state, what it covers, what it misses, and why it is the strongest layer available — free, and irreversible on purpose.
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-08-10

Short answer: Self-exclusion means telling operators to close your accounts and refuse you service for a fixed term. In the UK, one free GAMSTOP registration covers every UK-licensed online operator for 6 months, 1 year or 5 years, and it does not lift automatically at the end. In the US, register with your state programme and with each sportsbook individually. It is free, it takes about twenty minutes, and unlike any app you cannot reverse it during a craving.

Every other layer is something you install and can uninstall. Self-exclusion is different: you hand the decision to someone else, and they will not give it back on demand. That is why it is the first thing worth doing, and the thing most people put off longest.

## UK: one registration, every licensed site
GAMSTOP is the national online self-exclusion scheme. It is free, takes a few minutes, and every operator licensed by the Gambling Commission to offer online gambling in Britain is required to participate. Once you're registered, they must close your accounts and refuse new ones.
- Choose your term: 6 months, 1 year or 5 years. Take 5 years. The reason to choose a short term is almost always the part of you that intends to come back.
- It doesn't expire quietly. Reaching the end date does not restore access by itself — you have to contact GAMSTOP and pass a cooling-off period first. Verify the current process on their site; it has been revised before.
- Register accurately. Matching is done on your details, so an old address or a variant spelling can leave an account uncovered. Include every email address you have gambled with.
- Betting shops are separate. GAMSTOP is online only, and says so — the in-person scheme is a different sign-up.

### The gap, stated honestly
GAMSTOP binds UK-licensed operators. It has no power over sites licensed elsewhere, and an entire SEO industry exists to put "casinos not on GAMSTOP" in front of people at the exact moment they are looking for a way around their own decision. Those operators sit outside UK consumer protection, dispute resolution and deposit safeguards.
Two things close that gap: a DNS-level blocker, which doesn't care whose licence a site holds, and a bank gambling block, which doesn't care what site you reached. Self-exclusion plus those two is the combination that actually holds.

## US: state scheme plus every operator
There is no national equivalent of GAMSTOP. Coverage is built in two layers:
- Your state programme. Most states with legal gambling run a voluntary self-exclusion list, administered by the gaming commission or lottery, often covering both casinos and licensed online operators in that state. Terms are typically one year, five years or lifetime. The National Council on Problem Gambling keeps a directory of state self-exclusion programmes.
- Each operator, individually. Every licensed sportsbook and casino app has a responsible-gaming section with self-exclusion or self-restriction. Do it for all of them, including the ones you have "stopped using" — a dormant funded account is the easiest relapse there is. (Quitting sports betting specifically has its own problem: the cue is the sport, and you can't self-exclude from that.)

Where you can, choose the longest term offered, and do it in one sitting rather than one operator a week. Momentum matters more than thoroughness here; you can add the ones you forgot tomorrow.

## Elsewhere
Several countries run national schemes — among them Sweden (Spelpaus), the Netherlands (Cruks), Denmark (ROFUS), Belgium (EPIS) and Australia (BetStop). If you're outside those, ask every operator you use directly for permanent self-exclusion; licensed operators almost everywhere are obliged to offer it. Gambling Therapy provides free online support internationally and can point you at what exists locally.

## What to expect after you do it
- Marketing should stop. Excluded customers must be removed from promotional contact. If an operator keeps emailing or texting you, that's a compliance failure worth reporting to the regulator — and worth doing, because those messages are engineered to arrive when you're vulnerable.
- Withdraw your balances first, or at least check what happens to them under each operator's terms.
- Expect a bad week. Removing the option tends to make the wanting louder before it makes it quieter. That's the withdrawal pattern, not a sign you chose wrong — here's the shape it usually takes.
- Tell one person. Self-exclusion is easier to keep when it isn't a secret, and secrecy is one of the heaviest parts of a gambling problem to carry alone. (If you're the person being told: what actually helps.)

## The uncomfortable question
If reading this you found yourself thinking "I'll do the six months, not the five years" — notice that. It is the most reliable signal in the whole process, and it is worth being honest with yourself about which part of you is doing the negotiating.

## Common questions

Q: How long does GAMSTOP last?
A: You choose 6 months, 1 year or 5 years. At the end of the term it does not switch off by itself — you have to contact GAMSTOP and pass a cooling-off period before access is restored. Check GAMSTOP's own current terms, because the reactivation process has changed before.

Q: Does GAMSTOP cover betting shops?
A: No. GAMSTOP is the online scheme, covering websites and apps of UK-licensed operators. Betting shops are a separate self-exclusion process, and GAMSTOP itself points people towards it.

Q: Can I gamble on sites not covered by GAMSTOP?
A: Technically yes, and that is the scheme's real weakness — it has no authority over operators outside the UK licence. There is an entire industry of 'non-GAMSTOP casino' sites built to catch people mid-relapse, and unlicensed operators offer no UK consumer protection at all. This is exactly the gap a DNS-level blocker covers.

Q: How do I self-exclude from a US sportsbook?
A: Each operator has a responsible-gaming section with a self-exclusion or self-restriction option, usually offering set terms. Do it per operator, and separately register with your state programme where one exists — the National Council on Problem Gambling maintains a directory of state schemes.

Q: Will self-exclusion hurt my credit score?
A: No. Self-exclusion is an agreement with gambling operators or a scheme they subscribe to. It is not a credit event and does not appear on a credit file.

# Support
URL: https://trysilex.com/support/
Language: en
Description: Help with Silex: subscriptions and cancelling, restoring a purchase, the DNS shield, the Safari blocker, and how to reach a human.

Email support@trysilex.com. One person reads it, so replies usually take a day and sometimes two. Please say which iPhone and which iOS version you're on.
If you are in crisis, don't wait for an email reply. The helplines at the bottom of this page are free, confidential and answer 24/7.

## Subscriptions
- Prices. $4.99 per week, or $49.99 per year with a 3-day free trial. Local prices follow Apple's regional pricing.
- Cancelling. Settings → your name → Subscriptions → Silex → Cancel Subscription. Deleting the app does not cancel the subscription.
- Trial. The annual plan's 3-day trial charges nothing up front, and the app notifies you on day 2, before it ends. Cancel any time before it ends and you pay nothing.
- Refunds are handled by Apple, not by us: reportaproblem.apple.com. We can't issue them, but tell us what went wrong anyway — it usually points at something worth fixing.
- If your subscription lapses, the safety tools keep working. The urge button, the helplines and lapse support are free forever.

## Protection layers that won't turn on

### The DNS shield
The shield installs an encrypted-DNS configuration so gambling domains fail to resolve in every app and browser. If it's stuck:
- Check it's actually enabled: Settings → General → VPN, DNS & Device Management → DNS → "Silex Shield" should be selected.
- A configuration profile from a work or school device-management system can outrank it. On a managed phone, the shield may be blocked entirely.
- It does not survive a factory reset or a new device — re-run the setup.

### The Safari blocker
Safari content blockers are opt-in per browser: Settings → Apps → Safari → Extensions → "Silex Site Blocker" → on. It only covers Safari. Other browsers need their own extension, which is precisely why the DNS shield exists.

### Honest limits
No iOS app can make itself impossible to remove, and Silex doesn't claim to. Anyone determined enough can delete a blocker in thirty seconds. That's why the app pushes you toward the layers you can't undo on impulse — operator self-exclusion and a bank-level gambling block — and why it suggests giving a Screen Time passcode to someone you trust.

## Feature requests and bugs
Both go to the same address. Requests that make the app better at helping people quit get built; requests that would make it more addictive to use don't.

## Press
support@trysilex.com. Screenshots, the app icon and factual detail about how the app works are available on request; there is no press kit yet.

## Common questions

Q: How do I cancel my Silex subscription?
A: On your iPhone: Settings → your name → Subscriptions → Silex → Cancel Subscription. Cancelling in Apple's settings is the only way to stop billing; deleting the app does not cancel anything.

Q: I paid but Silex still shows the paywall.
A: Open the paywall and tap Restore Purchases, and check you are signed into the same Apple Account you bought with. If it still fails, email support@trysilex.com with the date of purchase.

Q: Why does the DNS shield need a profile?
A: Blocking gambling in every app and browser, not just Safari, requires an encrypted-DNS configuration at the system level. iOS asks you to approve it in Settings. You can remove it at any time from Settings → General → VPN, DNS & Device Management.

Q: Does deleting the app delete my data?
A: Yes, on the device. If iCloud backup was on, also remove the iCloud copy: Settings → your name → iCloud → Manage Account Storage → Silex.

Description: The terms for the Silex app, this website's free tools, the browser extension and the Notion recovery tracker. Short, plain, and honest about what Silex is not.

Last updated: 29 October 2026.
These terms cover everything called Silex: the iPhone app, the free tools on trysilex.com, the free browser extension, and the free Notion recovery tracker. They're short on purpose.

## 1. Who we are
Silex is made by one person, Kyrylo Lozovyi, in Kyiv, Ukraine. Contact: support@trysilex.com.

## 2. Silex is not medical care
Silex is a self-help tool. It doesn't diagnose or treat gambling disorder or any other condition, and it isn't a crisis service. Nothing in it is medical, legal or financial advice. If you're in danger or thinking about harming yourself, call your local emergency number or one of the free helplines listed on every page of this site.

## 3. Blocking is a help, not a guarantee
No blocker catches every gambling site or app, and any blocker can be removed by the person who installed it. The app, the extension and the website's lists are built in good faith and updated, but we can't promise that something won't get through. Self-exclusion with operators and your bank is the stronger layer, and our self-exclusion guide explains how.

## 4. The app and subscriptions
The app is distributed through Apple's App Store. Subscriptions are sold, billed, renewed and refunded by Apple, under Apple's terms, and are cancelled in your Apple Account settings. Deleting the app doesn't cancel a subscription. Prices and the free trial are shown in the app before you buy, and on the support page. Unless the App Store listing shows a different licence, the app is licensed to you under Apple's standard end user licence agreement.

## 5. The free tools
The website's self-check and calculators, the browser extension and the Notion recovery tracker are free. You can use them as much as you like, for yourself or to help someone else. When you connect the Notion tracker, you're asking us to create pages in your Notion workspace; those pages are yours, and what you write in them is between you and Notion. How each tool handles data is in the privacy policy.

## 6. Fair use
Please don't try to break, overload or reverse-engineer our services to harm others, or use them to promote gambling. The articles on this site may be quoted and linked with credit; please don't republish them in full as your own.

## 7. As-is, and the limits of our responsibility
Silex is provided as it is, without warranties, to the extent the law allows. To the extent the law allows, we aren't liable for indirect losses, or for losses caused by a site or app the blocker didn't catch. Nothing in these terms limits rights you have under consumer law that can't be limited by contract.

## 8. Changes
